waypoints.name: Killen Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Reached on Forest Roads 23, 21 and 2329 from the Randle or Trout Lake side. FR-2329 holds snow well into early summer, so check the road before committing — parties blocked short of the trailhead have had to walk or bushwhack an extra mile or more of road and forest to reach it.

waypoints.name: High Camp Trail Junction
waypoints.directions: Follow Killen Creek Trail #113 up through subalpine forest and meadow for about three miles to the Pacific Crest Trail, and cross straight over onto the High Camp Trail. Killen Creek, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable running water; everything above is melted snow. The tread thins out above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark or a whiteout, so note landmarks on the way up or carry a track.

waypoints.name: High Camp
waypoints.directions: Another mile on the High Camp Trail ends it at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine. Sheltered bivy sites sit slightly higher, in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine, and more camping is scattered across the benches above that.

waypoints.name: Adams Glacier Base
waypoints.directions: A patchy path runs past the upper camping area and up moraine and snow to the glacier toe, where parties rope up. Judge the timing generously — the volcano's scale flattens distance out and this leg routinely runs two hours. The point of the very early start is to be through the icefall before the sun starts working on it.

waypoints.name: Mount Adams Summit
waypoints.directions: The usual line takes the right-hand side of the glacier for roughly the first two-thirds, threading ice steps and serac lanes, then cuts back left high up onto the unbroken snow of the summit plateau. Which side of the upper icefall goes changes from year to year, and the left-hand option has been found far steeper than the grade suggests — sustained 55 to 65 degrees rather than moderate — so look at it in daylight from below before committing. The crossing beneath the ice cliffs is the stretch to move through fastest, on thin bridges and with backtracking common. Above the icefall the angle eases and two or three false summits stand between you and the true one, so keep navigating rather than trusting the first high point.

waypoints.name: Libby Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FS Road 4340-750; roadside parking for ~10 cars, no facilities — start of Libby Creek Trail #415.
waypoints.directions: Drive Libby Creek Road to its end at FS Road 4340-750, where the Libby Lake Trailhead — also called the Libby Creek Trailhead — sits at about 4,400 ft. Parking is roadside for roughly ten cars, with no facilities. No fee or pass is required here. Libby Creek Trail No. 415 starts from the road end and heads southwest into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness.

waypoints.name: Burn-zone spring
waypoints.note: Reliable spring 0.6 mile into the patchwork 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire burn scar; last easy water before the wilderness boundary.

waypoints.name: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness boundary
waypoints.note: Signed wilderness entry 0.3 mile past the spring; trail continues climbing through mixed burned/live forest.

waypoints.name: North Fork Libby Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford the North Fork of Libby Creek; an established campsite on the far bank is the last reliable water before the cabin.

waypoints.name: Historic trapper's cabin
waypoints.note: Decaying cabin where the scramble route leaves Libby Creek Trail; a faint boot path angles right (west) into the trees toward Hoodoo.

waypoints.name: Base of Hoodoo's boulder field
waypoints.note: Boot path fades crossing scree and lingering snow patches west of the cabin; from here it's choose-your-own-line up loose talus to gain the ridge — no defined tread.

waypoints.name: Hoodoo Peak
waypoints.note: Class 2 boulder scramble along the summit ridge to the register; many blocks are unstable, test holds before weighting them.

waypoints.name: Entiat River Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk; start of Entiat River Trail #1400.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Entiat River Road (FR 51) to its end at the Cottonwood Camp trailhead. Early in the season the road can be gated or still snowed in below the trailhead, which adds several miles of road walking or biking before the trail even starts — confirm access before committing to the drive.

waypoints.name: Anthem Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks here; stay on Entiat River Trail #1400 continuing up-valley.
waypoints.directions: Two easy miles up-valley on well-graded trail beside the river. Stay on #1400 where Anthem Creek Trail #1435 splits off; the Anthem crossing a short way beyond is on a solid bridge.

waypoints.name: Snow Brushy Creek to Aurora Creek
waypoints.note: Reliable creek crossings in an otherwise arid stretch of trail; refill here.
waypoints.directions: About four more miles of gentle valley trail, passing the Cow Creek/Myrtle Lake, Larch Lakes and Emerald Park junctions in turn — stay on #1400 at each one. The trail starts entering old burn scars along here, so shade thins and the tread turns dry and dusty.

waypoints.name: Candy Creek deadfall zone
waypoints.note: Heavy downed-tree debris from the 2015 Wolverine Fire begins past this point, slowing travel considerably.
waypoints.directions: Four more miles through repeated burn zones with almost no shade — the hottest and most exposed part of the approach, and dry between the creeks behind you and the meadows ahead. Pass the Ice Creek Trail junction along the way and keep on #1400.

waypoints.name: Cool Creek junction
waypoints.note: Trail junction below Buckskin Mountain marking the approach to the upper meadows.
waypoints.directions: The valley opens into Entiat Meadows on this stretch and water becomes reliable again. Travel is slow through the downed timber; step over it where you can, since the detours around it are what lose the tread.

waypoints.name: Entiat Meadows camp (5,100' clearing)
waypoints.note: Established camp in the open meadow clearing below the Fernow-Buckskin cirque; mosquitoes swarm mid-morning and afternoon.
waypoints.directions: Past the junction the trail grows faint and choked with brush and deadfall as it nears timberline. Keep going to the open clearing rather than settling lower — camping here is what keeps the summit day short. This is also the last dependable water; there is nothing above once you leave the trail except early-season snowmelt.

waypoints.name: South-face avalanche/scree gully
waypoints.note: Ascend the rib closest to camp up scree and heather; snow-covered early season and prone to sluffing after storms.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at camp and head straight up the broad old avalanche path on the south side. Several parallel ribs and gullies run up this face; the one closest to camp carries the least brush and gives the most direct line. An old boot path toward the east ridge appears on some maps but is buried in downed timber and is not worth hunting for.

waypoints.name: Buckskin Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit reached via the east ridge; watch for corniced sections and gendarmes just below the top.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly 2,000-2,800 ft of loose scree and heather, keeping close in under the buttress to stay out of the rockfall line, and gain the east ridge somewhere around 7,900 ft. From there a few hundred feet of narrow, blocky crest with minor gendarmes — and cornices on it into early summer — leads to the top. The whole face is exposed with nowhere to shelter, so plan to be off it before afternoon storms build.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack River Bridge / FR 38 Gate
waypoints.note: Gated bridge on FR 38 (Dailey Quarry Road) off Mosquito Lake Road; park at the gate even if open; no parking permit is needed, but the private timberland road beyond requires the landowner's fee access permit, and many parties bike it.
waypoints.directions: From WA-542, turn onto Mosquito Lake Road and follow it to FR-38 (the Dailey Quarry Road), then take FR-38 to its end at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, around 1,200 feet. Park at the gate even if you find it open — no permit is required to park here, though the road is closed to vehicles beyond this point and most parties continue from here by mountain bike.

waypoints.name: Dailey Prairie
waypoints.note: Old logging/quarry road passes this open prairie flat (a DNR Natural Area Preserve) before dropping into the basin between the Twin Sisters.
waypoints.directions: Ride or walk the old quarry and logging roads up from the gate. The grade is easy but the network branches repeatedly and the correct fork is rarely the obvious one, so follow a recorded track rather than instinct. Wrong turns here are the most common way to lose time on this route.

waypoints.name: Orsino Creek Crossing
waypoints.note: Last reliable water on the route; climbers' path crosses here and most parties stash bikes at this point before continuing on foot.
waypoints.directions: Past the prairie the roadbed drops into the basin between the two Sisters, taking a succession of left-hand forks as it goes. The road deteriorates until it is too rough or overgrown to ride, usually marked by a large culvert pipe where the timber road ends. Stash bikes in the trees and fill water at the crossing, because this is the last reliable source on the route.

waypoints.name: Orsino Creek Basin / Red Talus Slope
waypoints.note: Brushy old road fades to a boot path through timber then a red talus field opening into the upper basin below the West Ridge; talus often snow-covered into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot heading southeast. It is brushy and wet in places but followable; it drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and simply ends at a red talus slope that often holds snow into midsummer. From the talus traverse up and right (south), over a timbered rib and past the ruins of an old log cabin, into the upper basin.

waypoints.name: West Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: Gain the West Ridge crest here, roughly 1,800 ft below the summit; higher up, from a second notch about 400 ft below the summit, a traverse right (south) leads to easier Class 2-3 gullies instead of the ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: Climb out of the basin on steep dirt, scree and talus toward the obvious low notch in the ridge above. Sight the notch from the basin floor before starting up, and expect poor footing the whole way; this is the least pleasant stretch of the day.

waypoints.name: Dihedral in the upper cliff band
waypoints.note: Prominent dihedral in the cliffy band around 6,500 ft, below the false summit that parties often mistake for the true top; loose, abrasive dunite rock and a couple of low-5th-class moves here if staying on the ridge crest rather than dropping to the south-face gullies.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge up from the notch, roughly two hours of class 2-3 scrambling that moves on and off the crest. The right (south) side is generally solid and the left side is looser, and holding strictly to the crest is harder than dropping slightly south to bypass steps. The dunite is abrasive and holds friction unusually well, but it is hard on hands and rope. The ridge steepens into a cliffy band around 6,500 ft where the large dihedral sits.

waypoints.name: South Twin Sister
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Twin Sisters Range; two USGS benchmark caps and a summit register are on top, with Mount Baker visible 10 miles to the northeast.
waypoints.directions: The first high point above the dihedral is not the top and carries no cairn or register. Continue along the crest a short distance, on the order of fifty yards, crossing talus and any lingering snow to the next high point, which holds the survey markers and the register. In fog this last short stretch is where parties stop short and turn around believing they have summited.

waypoints.name: Hoh River Trailhead (Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center)
waypoints.note: Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center trailhead; shared start for multiple Mount Olympus routes.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the 23-mile Cascade River Road out of Marblemount; NPS wilderness permit (with bear canister for overnight) required, no day-use fee inside the park.
waypoints.directions: The final miles of Cascade River Road out of Marblemount are unpaved and washboarded, and high clearance or AWD makes the drive to the road end considerably easier.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass and turns east toward Pelton/Horseshoe Basin; a signed spur drops 1 mi and 800 ft to Doubtful Lake below the Sahale Arm.
waypoints.directions: Take the Cascade Pass Trail's well-graded switchbacks up the valley headwall, about 1,800 ft of gain on the only fully maintained tread of the route. Everything above the pass is unmaintained, loose and cairn-marked by comparison, so cover this section efficiently.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: Highest established backcountry camp in the park, at the base of Sahale Glacier; wind-wall rock sites, reservable NPS permit required, snowmelt water only early season.
waypoints.directions: Continue past the pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail and climb the open heather ridge, passing the Doubtful Lake overlook, to the camp at the toe of the glacier. It is a steady 2,200 ft of exposed, shadeless climbing with no water until you reach camp.

waypoints.name: Secret Gully descent off Sahale Arm
waypoints.note: Climbers' descent gully dropping east off the Sahale Arm into Horseshoe Basin; loose rock on slabs and unstable underfoot once snow-free.
waypoints.directions: From camp, traverse east across the boulder-and-heather plateau below the glacier, passing the dozen or so established camp pads, then downclimb a steep snowfield that can stay firm or icy into midsummer — an axe or whippet earns its place here. Traverse east again to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge, then follow the cairned climbers' trail down the ridge over one short 4th-class step to where the gully drops away east.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Basin staging area
waypoints.note: Waterfall-lined cirque beneath Ripsaw Ridge between Boston Peak and Buckner; stage here before the scramble up to Horseshoe Peak's south-facing gully.
waypoints.directions: Descend the scree-and-talus gully to the snowfield at about 6,600 ft and cross it into the basin. Melted out, the gully is loose mostly-3rd-class ground that needs real care; with snow still in it the concern shifts to steep firm snow instead. In the basin, traverse the wide ledge at roughly 6,600 ft as it rises toward the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine near 6,800 ft. Do not drink the basin's water — it drains historic mine tailings, so carry what you need from Doubtful Creek or camp.

waypoints.name: Summit gully and ledge
waypoints.note: 30-45° loose gully climbs to a ledge about 100 ft below the true summit, directly below the final 5.2 notch.
waypoints.directions: Contour northeast and then east on loose scree, talus and slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge under the peak, then start up the Class 3 dike-and-gully system. A short Class 4 step breaks it partway up. The whole line is loose enough that another party above you is the main hazard, so wear a helmet and keep the group either tight or well out of the fall line.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Peak
waypoints.note: True summit gained by ~5 ft of 5th-class climbing to a one-meter-square notch (feels overhung but isn't); downclimb or single-rope rappel to reverse.
waypoints.directions: From the ledge, scramble about 10 ft of Class 3/4 onto a ledge that angles diagonally up the south face to an obvious cleft just below the top, exiting on loose Class 3/4 rock at the notch. The final moves are 5.2 over fall-would-be-fatal exposure, so most parties rope the ramp as one pitch of roughly 30 m and belay off the horn on the east side of the notch. That horn is also the rappel anchor on the way down; it is natural rock with no fixed hardware, so carry a few cams in case the sling is missing or worn.

waypoints.name: Duckabush Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee required at this vault-toilet trailhead; overnight parties need an Olympic NP wilderness permit once the trail crosses the park boundary.

waypoints.name: Five Mile Camp
waypoints.note: Established riverside camp along the Duckabush River Trail; reliable river water, treat before drinking.

waypoints.name: Ten Mile Camp
waypoints.note: Last established campsite before the trail turns south for La Crosse Pass; sits at 1,400 ft with river water nearby.

waypoints.name: La Crosse Pass Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Duckabush River Trail forks here onto the La Crosse Pass Trail, which immediately switchbacks steeply up the valley wall toward the pass.

waypoints.name: La Crosse Pass
waypoints.note: No water at the pass (dry for miles either direction); leave the maintained trail here and start the cross-country climb north across heather and talus toward the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Mount La Crosse
waypoints.note: True summit reached via open heather benches and talus on the broad ridge crest, Class 2-3; best climbed mid-July through September before snow returns.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard, single approach for all Southern Pickets/Terror Basin objectives including Little Mac Spire.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Crossings
waypoints.note: Trail fords two branches of Goodell Creek that run high on hot afternoons; a small streamside campsite sits near the second crossing.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Cairn / Climbers' Path
waypoints.note: Large cairn and stone arrow mark the turn off the maintained Goodell Creek trail onto the steep, faint climbers' path south of Terror Creek — the start of the '~4,000 ft over 2 mi' push.

waypoints.name: Rocky Streambed Source
waypoints.note: Last dependable water on the climbers' path, running in a rocky streambed; the faint tread resumes just upstream.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Notch
waypoints.note: Gap on the east rim of Terror Basin reached via a rising traverse over moderate snow into midsummer; first view down onto the basin and the McMillan/Little Mac group.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Shared high camp for the whole McMillan/Terror cluster — flat gravel benches, running water, and rock-walled bivy sites; base for Little Mac, East Mac, and West Mac.

waypoints.name: Loose Rock Below the Summit Block
waypoints.note: Southern Pickets rock is notoriously fractured here; test holds and stagger climbers on the 5.4 pitches to avoid knocking rock onto partners below.

waypoints.name: Little Mac Spire
waypoints.note: Approximate — no independently surveyed summit coordinate found for this minor Southern Pickets spire; cross-referenced against neighboring McMillan/Terror group summits and the route's recorded approach track to place it as close to the true high point as possible.

waypoints.name: Foggy Dew Trailhead (FR 4340-200, Trail #417)
waypoints.note: Coordinate and elevation as published by the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest for the Foggy Dew Trailhead, where Foggy Dew Trail #417 begins. The Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead (4,740 ft) is ~2.9 mi away: Eagle Lakes Trail #431 runs to Martin and Cooney Lakes and never passes Foggy Dew Falls, which is the next waypoint here. Every recorded distance on this route is consistent with this trailhead and impossible from the other.

waypoints.name: Foggy Dew Falls
waypoints.note: Steep switchback section passes a two-tiered cascade in a narrow cleft; last easy, reliable water before the trail breaks into open basin country.

waypoints.name: Merchants Basin / Cooney Lake Trail #434 split
waypoints.note: Trail #417 tops out of timber into the open, wildflower-covered Merchants Basin below Sawtooth Ridge, where the Cooney Lake Trail #434 splits off toward Cooney Lake.

waypoints.name: Cooney Lake
waypoints.note: Larch-rimmed alpine lake with established camps near the outlet; last reliable water before climbing to the pass.

waypoints.name: Cooney Pass
waypoints.note: 7,900 ft saddle on Switchback's southeast side gains the crest of the Southeast Ridge, with views down into Merchants Basin and toward Sunrise Lake.

waypoints.name: Southeast Ridge scramble
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 rock scramble up loose, exposed talus/blocks on the ridge crest to the summit block; expect strong, cold wind near the top.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Roadside pullout on the north side of SR-20 near milepost 126.8, just east of Gorge Lake; day hiking needs no permit, but overnight camps in the park require a backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
waypoints.directions: The Pyramid Lake Trailhead is a signed gravel pullout on the north side of SR-20 near milepost 126.8, about 21 miles east of Marblemount and 6.4 miles past Newhalem, just past the Diablo turnoff at roughly 1,150-1,200 ft. The maintained Pyramid Lake Trail starts across the highway from the pullout. Day hiking needs no permit, but an overnight camp in the park does: pick up the NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center on your way through.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Lake
waypoints.note: Small landslide-dammed tarn with floating carnivorous sundew mats reached via well-graded trail; camping is prohibited at the lake or along the trail corridor, so treat it as a water stop only.
waypoints.directions: The Pyramid Lake Trail is maintained the whole way and climbs at a steady grade through old-growth forest, about 1,500 ft over 2.1 miles with no navigational decisions to make. Rock-hop the creek at roughly the 1-mile mark. That crossing and the lake itself are the last easy water you pass, because the climbers' path above offers almost nothing for the next several hours.

waypoints.name: Point 4555' / Pyramid Peak east ridge
waypoints.note: Boot path leaves the lakeshore and climbs a steep, often overgrown climber's trail (slide alder, class 2-3 rock and dirt) onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge; easy to lose in fog or on lingering snow.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly 2,000 ft in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge near 4,000 ft, then follows the narrow, knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Lingering snow or cloud on that crest is where parties lose the line.

waypoints.name: Colonial Glacier moraine camp
waypoints.note: Established tent sites on the terminal-moraine benches above the shrinking Colonial Glacier's meltwater tarn; last reliable camping before the col, exposed to wind.
waypoints.directions: Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it. Drop slightly off the ridge and traverse across scree and boulders, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and its meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water; the ground is open and takes the wind.

waypoints.name: Colonial-Neve col
waypoints.note: Broad saddle gained by a short 30-degree snow climb around the moraine lake; rope up for glacier travel here before dropping onto the Neve Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Rope up before leaving camp, as the Colonial Glacier is crevassed. Climb it south past the east flank of Paul Bunyan's Stump on snow up to about 30 degrees, working around the moraine lake, to the broad col near 6,840 ft. A stream at the col makes it a usable second camp and water source.

waypoints.name: Neve Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Roped traverse of one of Washington's largest non-volcanic glaciers toward Snowfield's NW ridge; crevasses are usually well-bridged by midsummer but require active route-finding around open slots.
waypoints.directions: From the col drop roughly 150-250 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped. The cleanest line runs through the centre of the crevasse field; bridges are usually sound by midsummer but need active route-finding around open slots and soften through the afternoon. There are very few visual reference points out here, so track your line for the return, because whiteout navigation is the standing problem on this crossing.

waypoints.name: West ridge / NW face gully
waypoints.note: Leave the glacier and gain the west ridge via a class 3 gully with an exposed rib crossing about 300-400 vertical feet below the summit.
waypoints.directions: Leave the glacier on Snowfield's northwest side near The Horseman, around 7,700 ft, and gain the west ridge by a class 3 gully with one exposed rib crossing. This puts you 300-400 vertical feet below the summit. Early in the season the rock through here can carry verglas or rime.

waypoints.name: Snowfield Peak
waypoints.note: True summit reached by a final class 3-4 blocky scramble; broad views over Colonial, Pyramid, and the peak's namesake permanent snowfields.
waypoints.directions: A long class 3 gully leads up to a notch just below the true summit, then a short exposed traverse onto the south side and a short stretch of blocky scrambling finishes it. One move is occasionally low class 4, and harder lines exist to either side, so stay on the easiest ground. You downclimb that notch on the way out, so read it as you pass.

waypoints.name: Snow Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: 4.2 mi south on Icicle Creek Rd (FR-76) from junction with US-2, Leavenworth.
waypoints.directions: From Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 4.2 to 4.3 miles to the Snow Lakes Trailhead, at roughly 1,350 feet. Park in the lot on the south side of the road at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Upper Dungeness / Royal Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large parking area at end of FR 2870 off Palo Alto Rd/FR 28; $5 NW Forest day-use fee, self-issue permit envelope, pit toilets.
waypoints.directions: Take Highway 101 to just before Sequim Bay State Park and turn onto Louella Road, then follow Palo Alto Road, which becomes Forest Road 28, for about 6 miles. Turn right on FR 2880 along the Dungeness River, and 1.7 miles later turn left on FR 2870 and stay on it for roughly 6.5 to 9 miles of gravel that winds steeply down to a river crossing. It ends at the large Dungeness/Royal Basin trailhead lot, with a picnic table and a vault toilet. There is a $5 Northwest Forest day-use fee, paid with the self-issue permit envelope at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Royal Creek / Dungeness River crossings
waypoints.note: Trail parallels and repeatedly crosses Royal Creek on log bridges after the first easy mile along the Dungeness River; reliable water throughout.

waypoints.name: Shelter Rock
waypoints.note: Massive overhanging rock on the left just below Royal Lake, a well-known trail landmark and informal rest stop.

waypoints.name: Royal Lake
waypoints.note: Designated backcountry campsites at the outlet; overnight permit and bear canister required, no campfires.

waypoints.name: Arrowhead Meadow
waypoints.note: Trail crosses a log bridge, climbs steeply, then levels into this open alpine meadow below Upper Royal Basin.

waypoints.name: Upper Royal Basin tarns
waypoints.note: First of several milky-blue tarns fed by snowmelt off the Needles; last reliable water before the talus climb.

waypoints.name: East flank talus/scree gully below the Needles
waypoints.note: Loose, unstable talus and scree on the exposed east side; rockfall risk increases with parties above, especially in shoulder-season conditions.

waypoints.name: Sundial summit block
waypoints.note: Final class 3 scramble up a short, exposed ridge-top pitch to the true summit; loose rock and steep drop-offs on the east side.

waypoints.name: Glacier Vista
waypoints.directions: Leave the upper Paradise lot on the Skyline Trail and follow the standard Muir-bound tread as it climbs above the meadows. Glacier Vista is the marked overlook where the Nisqually opens up several hundred feet below you. This is where the Kautz route leaves the trail system for good.

waypoints.name: Wilson Gully (Crux)
waypoints.directions: Follow the climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, then drop onto the Nisqually and rope up before starting across — the crossing threads crevassed terrain under icefall and is genuinely dangerous in poor visibility. Take the line of least resistance over to the far side and the distinct low-angle snow gully there, then climb it to the bench above at roughly 7,300 to 7,400 ft. Move through this stretch early and do not stop in it.

waypoints.name: Camp Hazard
waypoints.directions: From the top of the gully follow the ridge line up past the string of established camps — Wilson Moraine, then Lower and Upper Castle, which is where most parties spend the first night and where running water is usually available from mid-June on. Above the Castle the Turtle snowfield leads to Camp Hazard: sun-cupped firm snow and glacier ice, so keep an ice tool in hand. Stay to the west side of the snowfield, because its centre and east flank are raked by rock and ice off the Kautz Ice Cliff.

waypoints.name: Columbia Crest
waypoints.directions: Leave camp in the dark. Drop a couple of hundred feet through the gully between the rock cliff and the ice cliff, then move left around the base of the ice cliff to the foot of the chute — this is the deposition zone under the ice cliff and the reason for the alpine start, so cross it moving. The chute is two steps of snow and ice separated by easier snow, each anything from a short pitch to a few hundred feet depending on the year, bare and hard in a lean year, and six to eight screws is a sensible rack. Above it, angle up the upper Kautz and Wapowety Cleaver, working around crevasses, moats along the rock, and a large bergschrund near the crater rim before the flat walk to the top.

waypoints.name: Paradise Parking Area
waypoints.directions: Paradise sits on the mountain's south side at about 5,400 ft, at the end of the Paradise road. The climb starts from the upper lot on the Skyline Trail.

waypoints.name: Skyline Trail / Muir Steps
waypoints.directions: Leave the upper lot on the paved Skyline Trail, which climbs immediately in stone steps behind the lodge — the bottom of the long grind to Camp Muir.

waypoints.name: Panorama Point
waypoints.directions: Skyline switchbacks up open slopes to Panorama Point, the standard first rest stop, with the view south over the Tatoosh Range to Mount Adams.

waypoints.name: Pebble Creek Crossing
waypoints.directions: Past Panorama Point the trail drops slightly to Pebble Creek at roughly 2.3 miles. This is the last reliable water on the way up, so fill here. McClure Rock (~7,385 ft) sits just above, and that is where the maintained trail ends.

waypoints.name: Camp Muir
waypoints.directions: Above McClure Rock the route becomes the Muir Snowfield — permanent snow, unmarked, and not maintained by the Park Service. Guide services boot-pack and wand it through the season, but wind and new snow erase the track fast, and whiteout navigation here has killed people. Carry map and compass or GPS and be able to use them before you rely on a boot-pack. Camp Muir at 10,080 ft has an NPS ranger station with weather briefings and current route conditions.

waypoints.name: Ingraham Flats High Camp
waypoints.directions: Rope up at Muir. Traverse the upper Cowlitz Glacier, then scramble the Cathedral Rocks ridge through Cathedral Gap — shorten the rope between partners here, because the switchbacks are awkward on a long one. Over the gap you drop onto the Ingraham Glacier and reach Ingraham Flats, the standard high camp at the foot of the Cleaver.

waypoints.name: High Crack Crevasse
waypoints.directions: Above the Flats the route crosses the Ingraham's crevasse field, where guide services install ladders and planks at High Crack and stitch a line together as the season opens the glacier up. This traverse runs beneath large overhanging seracs — move through it quickly and do not stop to regroup underneath them. The exact line changes year to year and within a season; fixed ladders and wands typically go in around mid-May and are pulled at the end of September, after which nothing on the upper mountain is fixed.

waypoints.name: Columbia Crest
waypoints.directions: Gain the Cleaver and climb the rock rib to its top around 12,300 ft. Rockfall is a genuine hazard here once the season warms, particularly after June, so helmets stay on and parties keep moving. Above the Cleaver the glacier is the most dynamic part of the route — climb as directly toward the east crater rim as the crevasses allow. From the rim, drop into the crater and cross it to the west side for Columbia Crest, the true summit. Most parties leave Camp Muir between about 10pm and 2am to reach the top early and be off the upper mountain before it softens; summit day is roughly 4,500-5,500 ft of gain.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134)
waypoints.note: North Cascades NP wilderness permit required; a 0.6-mile spur trail drops to the Ross Lake shoreline where the multi-day approach to Castle Peak begins.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is a pullout on SR-20 near milepost 134. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required before you start.

waypoints.name: Ross Lake Dock / Boat Put-in
waypoints.note: Put-in for the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (or paddle) that shortcuts many miles of the East Bank Trail toward the Lightning Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: A 0.6-mile spur trail drops from the pullout to the Ross Lake shoreline, losing about a hundred feet. Anyone bringing a private or inflatable boat portages it down this stretch.

waypoints.name: Lightning Creek Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Boat drop-off where the route leaves Ross Lake and picks up the Lightning Creek Trail heading east into the valley toward Freezeout Creek.
waypoints.directions: The lake crossing runs north to the Lightning Creek landing near the head of Ross Lake. The resort water taxi is the usual way across and books out well in advance; paddling it adds hours at both ends. Either way the return pickup is a fixed time, so plan the summit day around it — there is no quick walk-out from this side.

waypoints.name: Turner Bridge / Nightmare Camp
waypoints.note: Lightning Creek crossing near Nightmare Camp on an aging span; the bridge is unstable and a ford may be required.
waypoints.directions: From the landing follow the Lightning Creek Trail up-valley for roughly seven miles of forest walking. Parties commonly leave the shore before dawn to leave enough daylight for the ground above. The bridge is the Lightning Creek crossing and has been in poor shape; a ford may be the safer option, and that is a call worth making in daylight on the way in rather than by headlamp on the way out.

waypoints.name: Freezeout Creek Cabin
waypoints.note: Maintained backcountry cabin at about 3,600 ft on the abandoned Freezeout Creek Trail, above the steep section where it leaves the Lightning Creek Trail; the last reliably stocked shelter/water stop before the climb proper.
waypoints.directions: Cross Lightning Creek and pick up the old, unmaintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that take a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and tread. Flagging has marked it in recent seasons but do not plan on it being there. Back in the trees the tread is in decent shape the rest of the way, and the cabin sits just past a creek crossing.

waypoints.name: Freezeout Creek Ford & Blowdown Zone
waypoints.note: Trail disintegrates into heavy blowdown above the cabin; climbers ford Freezeout Creek and sidehill through alder to regain open talus near 5,000 ft.
waypoints.directions: About a quarter mile above the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly gives out near 4,200 ft where it turns north and re-crosses the creek, though the bushwhacking through here is not bad. Stay on the west side of the creek roughly 50-100 ft above the water — that band gives the most open going — until about 5,000 ft, where you cross to the south/east side and the ground opens into meadow and talus.

waypoints.name: Southwest Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: Gained via steep red heather and scree slopes; marks the start of the class 2-3 scramble along the SW ridge to the summit.
waypoints.directions: From the open ground above 5,000 ft it is a long, steady climb on steep red heather, talus and scree to the notch — around 2,500 ft of gain with no water on any of it, so fill from the creek before you leave it. Several similar-looking gullies and chutes feed this basin; note the exact one you come up, because taking the wrong one on the way down cliffs you out on bluffs well above the creek.

waypoints.name: Castle Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit, second-highest peak in the Hozomeen Range, about one mile south of the Canadian border; class 2-3 scrambling on the final pitch.
waypoints.directions: From the notch it is roughly 700 vertical feet along the ridge, mostly Class 2 with short Class 3 steps. The rock is generally good but there is loose talus on it, and the crest is fully exposed with nowhere to shelter — get off it early if storms are building. On this schedule most parties finish the descent in the dark, so carry headlamps regardless of the forecast.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road)
waypoints.note: Sol Duc trailhead at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road, the start of the High Divide / Bailey Range approach. Whiskey Bend is 11.7 mi away on the Elwha and approaches Mount Barnes from the opposite end, never passing Heart Lake — the first waypoint here. Every recorded distance on this route is consistent with a Sol Duc start.

waypoints.name: Heart Lake
waypoints.note: Last reliable water and common camp before crossing High Divide; there is no water again until well past the Catwalk toward Eleven Bull Basin.

waypoints.name: High Divide crest near Bogachiel Peak
waypoints.note: Maintained High Divide Trail tops out here; this is where the Bailey Range Traverse leaves the trail and drops off-trail east into Cat Basin toward Cat Peak. The exact off-trail departure point is not recorded separately, so this marker sits on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk (Cat Peak-Mt. Carrie arete)
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed ridgeline with a few scrambling moves and roughly 3,000 ft of air to the valley floor; poorly defined in fog, not a place to be in wind or wet rock.

waypoints.name: Upper Ferry Basin / Ferry Glacial Lake
waypoints.note: Open meadow below Mount Ferry with glacial lakes and streams for the last dependable water before the Bear Pass approach; established informal camp used by most Bailey Range parties.

waypoints.name: Childs Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Small glacier/permanent snowfield below Bear Pass; parties report needing ice axe and microspikes on firm snow, with crevasse-type terrain in Junkyard Basin just beyond.

waypoints.name: Bear Pass
waypoints.note: Broad saddle marking the southeastern terminus of the Bailey Range proper; from here the route drops toward a flat meadow before angling southeast for the final Barnes approach.

waypoints.name: North Fork Entiat Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 5606; self-issue Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee kiosk at the lot, day-use only with no camping at the TH itself.

waypoints.name: Fern Lake Trail (#1436) junction
waypoints.note: Trail #1437 tops a switchbacking climb away from the river here where the short Fern Lake spur splits off; stay on #1437 toward the Pyramid Mtn Trail rather than detouring to the lake.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1437 runs up the North Fork Entiat valley for about six miles, mostly gentle beside the river before switchbacks lift you away from it. The tread carries a reputation for blowdown, so budget time for it even when reports say it is clear.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Mountain Trail (#1433) junction camp
waypoints.note: Flat clearing where Trail #1437 meets the Pyramid Mtn Trail; a nearby log/plank crossing has been reported to flex badly in high water and is the usual base camp before heading off-trail toward Saska Pass.
waypoints.directions: Roughly two and a half miles on from the Fern Lake spur, staying on #1437. Fill water at the crossing here: the drainages between this junction and the pass are seasonal and are often dry.

waypoints.name: Saska Pass
waypoints.note: Gain the pass off-trail via a steep dry streambed and a loose scree headwall; it marks the crest between the Emerald Peak basin and the Snow Brushy Creek burn drainage leading to Pinnacle's north side.
waypoints.directions: Leave the tread before it starts traversing toward the pass and climb the drainage directly; the traverse sidehills across scree and is slower and more tiring than going straight up. The headwall above the bench is loose enough to be worth a helmet, and it is worse for anyone climbing below you.

waypoints.name: Snow Brushy Creek burn-zone crossing
waypoints.note: Descend roughly 1,500 ft off the pass into the 2006/2015-era burn; ash-covered slopes and heavy standing/fallen burnt snags erase the tread, so carry a GPS track rather than relying on cairns.
waypoints.directions: Head straight down the far side of the pass rather than hunting for tread, because none survives here. The burn is open enough that the descent goes quickly, but every foot of it has to be regained on the way home, and the far bank climbs steeply straight out of the creek.

waypoints.name: Basin below Pinnacle's summit block
waypoints.note: Exit the burn into open larch basins on the peak's north side, then climb loose scree to a bench that sets up the final class 2-3 ridge traverse to the summit.
waypoints.directions: A steep and unrelenting climb of around 1,900 feet out of the creek: poor scree low down where the burn ends, easing as the ground opens higher up. This leg and the reclimb of the pass afterwards are what make the day long, not any difficulty on the peak itself.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit (8,400 ft), first climbed 1948 by Dwight Watson and Ken Fleming; the standard finish is class 3 scrambling up the south-slope talus, which doubles as the descent line.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest on from the bench, keeping to its west side where the scrambling stays easiest. The rock here is noticeably more solid than the scree below, but it is still a hands-on class 3 finish rather than a walk-up.

waypoints.name: Park Butte / Schreiber's Meadow
waypoints.directions: Drive to the end of Forest Road 13 (Sulfur Creek Road), which ends at the Park Butte / Schreiber's Meadow trailhead at about 3,360 feet. From the parking area, pick up Park Butte Trail 603 and cross Sulfur Creek on a footbridge or log crossing near the start — this can become a genuine ford during peak snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Park Butte Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FS Road 13; a recreation pass is required to park and is not sold at the lot, so buy it ahead or pay by phone; start up Park Butte Trail 603.
waypoints.directions: Reach the Park Butte Trailhead at the end of Forest Service Road 13, via the Baker Lake Highway and the Sulfur Creek Road turnoff. Park at the trailhead lot; a recreation pass is required and is not sold on site, so buy it ahead or pay by phone. No wilderness permit is needed.

waypoints.name: Sulphur Creek crossing, Schriebers Meadow
waypoints.note: Ford Sulphur Creek on a log/plank crossing at the edge of Schriebers Meadow, then turn north toward Railroad Grade; last reliable running water before high camp.

waypoints.name: Railroad Grade Trail 603.2 junction
waypoints.note: Park Butte Trail splits here; leave it for Railroad Grade Trail 603.2, which climbs directly onto the crest of the lateral moraine.

waypoints.name: Sandy Camp
waypoints.note: Terminus of Railroad Grade Trail and the standard high camp for the Easton Glacier route; last established, durable tent sites before glacier travel.

waypoints.name: Easton Glacier toe / rope-up point
waypoints.note: Rope up for glacier travel here; head northwest toward the crater rim, weaving around open crevasses and snow bridges on the lower Easton Glacier.

waypoints.name: Sherman Crater rim / Sherman Peak spur
waypoints.note: Sulfur smell from active fumaroles vents near the crater rim; a short spur off the main Easton Glacier line leads to the Sherman Peak high point instead of continuing to Grant Peak.

waypoints.name: Sherman Peak summit
waypoints.note: False-summit high point on Mount Baker's crater rim, just south of and lower than the true summit (Grant Peak, 10,781 ft).

waypoints.name: Boston Basin / Cascade River Road trailhead
Forbidden Peak summit / rappel horn
waypoints.note: Start of the descent: locate the rappel horn/anchor near the true summit.

waypoints.name: First of 5 rappels
waypoints.note: Approximate position - five single-rope rappels (~400 ft total) down the NE side to reach the ledge system. Coordinates are estimated; no public GPS track exists for this line.

waypoints.name: Ledge traverse begins
waypoints.note: Mostly 3rd class ledges; stay well below the ridge crest, working east.

waypoints.name: Rock rib crossings (~5 ribs)
waypoints.note: Short 4th-class moves at each rib crossing; cairns (a higher and lower option at each rib) mark the easiest line. Position is approximate/estimated.

waypoints.name: Gully back to ridge crest
waypoints.note: A short gully leads back up to the East Ridge crest near the solitary gendarme.

waypoints.name: Rejoin East Ridge / gully descent to Boston Basin
waypoints.note: From the gendarme, descend the East Ridge's standard gully system back toward Boston Basin and camp.

waypoints.name: Kindy Creek Road (FR-1570) Y-junction parking
waypoints.note: From Marblemount drive 14.2 mi up Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River on a concrete bridge onto FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road), and park at the Y-junction; the spur beyond is rough and often blocked to vehicles.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road about 14.2 miles from Marblemount and turn right onto FR-1570, Kindy Creek Road, which crosses the Cascade River on a concrete bridge. Within roughly 0.4 mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout, and parking is at that Y-junction, around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two-to-three mile road walk rather than a trailhead. June through September is the working window.

waypoints.name: Blocked road ends, climbers' path begins
waypoints.note: After roughly 3 miles walking the deteriorating FR-1570 spur, an unmarked climbers' path breaks left into the trees and climbs very steeply — easy to lose, especially descending in fog.
waypoints.directions: Walk the closed roadbed uphill for two to three miles through windfall and encroaching brush; two large washouts cut it and can be awkward when snowmelt is running high. The road ends at a small clearing with an old firepit. The climbers' path leaves on the left near that clearing, unsigned and steep from its first step, so fix the spot in your mind on the way in, because it is much harder to find from above in fog on the way out.

waypoints.name: Boggy meadow low camp
waypoints.note: First flat ground with seasonal boggy water on the ridge, used by parties splitting the approach into two days before pushing on toward Found Peak.
waypoints.directions: The path climbs hard and unrelentingly, first through brush and then into old growth, on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock. There is no water on this section, so carry what you need from below. The grade finally eases at a boggy bench with room for a tent, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.

waypoints.name: Found Peak saddle / Found Lake fisherman's trail fork
waypoints.note: A fisherman's trail forks west here toward Found Lake; stay on the climbers' path and traverse below Peak 5116 rather than going directly over it.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge up from the bench. The tread is faint through grass and boulders on this stretch and parties routinely lose it, picking it up again a few hundred feet higher; when in doubt stay on the crest. The fork sits on the saddle and is marked by a cairn rather than a sign.

waypoints.name: Cyclone Lake meadows
waypoints.note: The most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites in the meadows below Peak 5791/5860; most overnight parties stage here for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Traverse on past the fork and continue along Kindy Ridge, dropping past the meadow that holds Found Lake and crossing the next small point to the saddle beyond. The line generally stays on the west side of the crest. Net elevation change is small but the ground rolls constantly, so it takes longer than the distance suggests.

waypoints.name: High camp on rock/snow benches
waypoints.note: Exposed benches below the Snowking Glacier used to shorten summit day; wind-exposed with limited flat tent space.
waypoints.directions: Work counterclockwise around the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A rock wall lines the east side of the outlet; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall directly. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the southwest, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto the slabs and benches.

waypoints.name: Crevassed section below the south notch
waypoints.note: The route crosses a crevassed stretch of the Snowking Glacier below the south notch — rope up and probe, particularly in late season when snow bridges are thin.
waypoints.directions: From the benches climb past the small tarns and traverse rocky slopes toward the notch, then take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier. Rope up before stepping onto the snow rather than partway across.

waypoints.name: Snowking Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via the easy east/southeast ridge with class 3 scrambling on the final blocks; broad views across the North Cascades Core.
waypoints.directions: Cross the glacier to the southwest, aiming straight at the peak, and leave the snow for rock on the left where a faint scree path picks up. The last of it is sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks, taken from the southeast ridge or the south slope. Time the return so you are back across the glacier before the afternoon sun softens the bridges.

waypoints.name: Upper Dungeness Trailhead
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead off FR 2870; Northwest Forest Pass required at the self-issue kiosk, and a wilderness permit is needed for Royal Basin camping.
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,550 ft at the end of FR 2870. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the self-issue kiosk, and Royal Basin camping needs a wilderness permit (quota season runs May through September).

waypoints.name: Royal Basin Trail junction
waypoints.note: Dungeness River Trail forks here; leave the river trail and climb south on the Royal Basin Trail toward Royal Creek.
waypoints.directions: Start on Upper Dungeness Trail 833.2, a gentle and nearly level mile through old growth alongside the Dungeness River to a well-signed fork. Leave the river trail and bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail, which climbs southwest up the Royal Creek valley.

waypoints.name: Royal Creek
waypoints.note: Trail parallels Royal Creek for several miles with multiple crossings; reliable water but can run high with snowmelt in early season.
waypoints.directions: Settle into a steady, moderate climb up the Royal Creek valley for roughly five miles, crossing several tributary creeks along the way. These are the last reliable water before the high basin and can run high with early-season snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Royal Lake designated camp
waypoints.note: Established sites with a composting toilet near the lake outlet; no campfires above 3,500 ft and bear canisters are required.
waypoints.directions: The forest opens into wildflower meadows around the six-mile mark, with the 7,000 ft summits of Mount Clark and Mount Walkinshaw in view ahead. The trail then steepens through switchbacks into Royal Basin to reach Royal Lake at 5,100 ft, about 7.2 miles in and 2,500 ft above the car. Established sites and a composting toilet sit near the outlet; bear canisters are required and no fires are allowed above 3,500 ft.

waypoints.name: Arrowhead Meadow
waypoints.note: Open meadow between Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin where the trail becomes fainter; watch for the climbers' path branching toward the basin's west side.
waypoints.directions: Above the lake a climbers' path crosses willow flats and boulder benches. Tread becomes fainter through this open meadow, so watch for the path branching toward the west side of the basin.

waypoints.name: Upper Royal Basin
waypoints.note: Seasonal ranger station and the last reliable water before heading cross-country; the Needles' craggy west wall rises directly above.
waypoints.directions: Continue on the climbers' path a total of roughly 0.8 to 1 mile and 500 ft of gain above Royal Lake to Upper Royal Basin at about 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Camping is not permitted in the upper basin, but it is the staging point for every Needles objective and holds the last reliable water before the cross-country travel, with the craggy west wall of the Needles rising directly above.

waypoints.name: East-face talus below the northeast col
waypoints.note: Loose, rotten Olympic shale on the talus and scree below the ridge; rockfall risk is high, especially with parties above — helmets recommended.
waypoints.directions: Beyond Upper Royal Basin there is no maintained tread. Traverse cross-country north, contouring on talus and boulder benches below Mount Clark's east flank toward Walkinshaw at the north end of the chain; this stretch adds roughly 1.5 miles of rough sidehill travel with several hundred feet of ascent and descent, and demands real route-finding since krummholz and short cliff bands hide the best line. Aim for the prominent talus tongue below the east face, then climb northwest over boulders and a bare scree rib to the col northeast of the peak, where loose, rotten Olympic shale makes rockfall the defining hazard, so keep the party tight and helmets on.

waypoints.name: Mount Walkinshaw summit
waypoints.note: Northernmost summit of the Needles, reached from the col northeast of the peak along the broken northeast ridge; Class 3 with perhaps one short Class 4 step; exposed, loose rock near the top.
waypoints.directions: From the col, skirt a few steepening pinnacles on their east side, then follow the northeast ridge through ledges and small gullies and along an airy blade to the small summit block roughly ten feet across at 7,378 ft. The rock is looser than typical Cascades granite, so test holds and keep the party out from under each other.

waypoints.name: North Fork Entiat River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 5606, about 35.3 mi from Entiat (32.3 mi on Entiat River Road/FR 51 + 3 mi on FR 5606); start of North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437, Northwest Forest Pass required with self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Glacier Peak Wilderness Boundary
waypoints.note: Trail crosses into Glacier Peak Wilderness here; stock/group-size rules apply beyond this point, no additional permit needed.
waypoints.directions: The first four miles of the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade on this stretch and the east-side valley bottom runs hot and dry in summer — carry more water than the mileage implies.

waypoints.name: Fox Camp (Pyramid Creek Trail junction)
waypoints.note: Established camp just off the North Fork Entiat trail where the Pyramid Creek Trail forks west; standard base camp for Saska/Emerald/Cardinal objectives.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the North Fork Entiat valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction; the camp itself sits about a quarter mile north of the junction. This junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start, so navigate by the drainage and the fork rather than by an odometer.

waypoints.name: Basin between Emerald and Saska
waypoints.note: 1.5 mi up the Pyramid Creek Trail from Fox Camp into the upper basin below Emerald and Saska; talus/snow camping, last reliable water before the col.
waypoints.directions: From the junction take the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb steadily for roughly a mile and a half into the upper basin. The tread is unmaintained and intermittent. Pushing to this camp instead of stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and takes about that much off the summit morning.

waypoints.name: Emerald-Saska col saddle
waypoints.note: Climb scree/talus (snow-filled gully early season) out of the basin to the notch on the ridge connecting Emerald and Saska; route splits toward either summit here.
waypoints.directions: Roughly 600 ft of gain out of the basin to the notch. Loose rock is the theme of this whole cirque — wear a helmet and avoid stacking the party directly above one another. In early-to-mid season continuous snow on this slope allows a glissade or boot-ski on the way back down; by August and September that is gone and the same ground becomes slow, controlled scree steps rather than good scree-skiing.

waypoints.name: Summit scree/talus gully
waypoints.note: Loose scree gully with Class 3 rock bands above the col; exposed and rockfall-prone, especially with other parties above on the south slopes.
waypoints.directions: Head west from the col toward Saska. The connecting crest is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line drops slightly onto its west flank to pick up an obvious scree-and-rock gully, then follows a cairned rising traverse back toward the crest. Everything underfoot moves — keep the party close together and out of each other's fall line.

waypoints.name: Saska Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Saska Peak (8,404 ft); broad views of Emerald and Cardinal Peaks and the North Fork Entiat headwaters.
waypoints.directions: Roughly 300 ft of final class 3 scrambling on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold: nothing is fixed and no rope is standard here, though the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them. This is the stretch that punishes a late finish or poor visibility on the way back down, so set your turnaround before you leave the col.

waypoints.name: Whiskey Bend Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of the Elwha River Trail (28.4 mi to Low Divide); the road to it has been closed to vehicles at the Madison Falls parking area since November 2017 flood damage, so it is reached on foot or by bike.

waypoints.name: Lillian River Trail junction
waypoints.note: Elwha River Trail crosses to the east bank near the Lillian River confluence and meets the Lillian River Trail spur; reliable water here before the climb to a high crest at mile 6.2.

waypoints.name: Mary's Falls Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry campsite beside the falls on the Elwha River Trail; NPS wilderness permit reservation required in summer season.

waypoints.name: Chicago Camp (Elwha ford)
waypoints.note: Ford (footlog when present) of the Elwha River just before the trail's steep 3.1 mi final push toward Low Divide; last established camp before leaving the maintained trail for Elwha Basin.

waypoints.name: Mount Dana
waypoints.note: Summit of Mount Dana, reached by following the ridge crest east and then northeast from the Barnes–Wilder ridge; class 2 scrambling at the top.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road, Forest Road 9737: from I-90 take exit 85 near Cle Elum onto SR 970 heading northeast, then follow the Teanaway River Road roughly 23 miles to the road-end parking at about 4,243 feet. The road is gravel and is not maintained through winter, typically staying snowed in until late June in a heavy year, so check conditions before an early-season trip.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Way Trailhead (North Fork Teanaway Rd, FR-9737) via Longs Pass
waypoints.note: Shared trailhead for Longs Pass Trail and Esmeralda Basin/Ingalls Way Trail; route drops from Longs Pass into Ingalls Creek drainage before climbing to Sherpa's east basin.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Fork Teanaway Road (FR-9737) to its end at the Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Way trailhead. This is the shared lot for the Longs Pass Trail and the Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Way Trail, and it is the same trailhead the West Ridge uses; for the East Ridge you want the Longs Pass Trail (FST 1391), which goes over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and down to Ingalls Creek. Plan on late June through September, once that Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek approach is snow-free.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 7601 past Eightmile Lake; self-issue day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk, Northwest Forest Pass required for parking.
waypoints.directions: The Stuart Lake Trailhead sits at the end of Eightmile Road (FR 7601), which leaves Icicle Creek Road (FR 7600); follow FR 7601 to its end, past Eightmile Lake. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park in the lot. Fill out the self-issue day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk before you start walking.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Continue straight on the Stuart Lake Trail past this junction, staying along Mountaineer Creek rather than turning left for Colchuck Lake.

waypoints.name: Off-trail turn toward Stuart Glacier basin
waypoints.note: About a mile past the Colchuck junction, leave the maintained trail and follow the valley climbers' path up toward the Sherpa/Stuart Glacier basin — often snow-covered and poorly marked March-June.

waypoints.name: Basin below Sherpa Glacier
waypoints.note: Standard base camp for the Stuart Glacier Couloir in a small flat valley at the base of the Sherpa Glacier, about 5 miles and 5+ hours from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Stuart Glacier Couloir bergschrund
waypoints.note: Bergschrund at the couloir's entrance around 7,800 ft is often the route's crux obstacle; parties have belayed across on sugary, unconsolidated snow.

waypoints.name: West Ridge notch (col)
waypoints.note: Couloir tops out at this notch on the West Ridge, the col shared with the West Ridge route, after a narrow ice/snow section that can run 40-60 degrees; continue over mixed 5th-class rock toward the summit.

waypoints.name: Mount Stuart summit
waypoints.note: True summit, typically reached via 2-3 short pitches of mid-5th-class rock above the West Ridge notch.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the kiosk; Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required for the lot.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Established lakeshore campsites and reliable water on the east shore where Pete Lake Trail #1323 meets the lake.
waypoints.directions: Four flat, forested miles on the Cooper River Trail #1323 with barely 200 ft of gain — the easiest walking of the trip, and no measure of what follows it.

waypoints.name: Lemah Meadow / PCT junction campsite
waypoints.note: Small campsite marks the Pacific Crest Trail junction; leave the maintained trail here and head west toward Lemah Meadows and the peak.
waypoints.directions: Continue along the shore past the lake camps for roughly another mile, staying left at each trail fork, to where the Pacific Crest Trail comes in.

waypoints.name: Lemah Meadows creek ford
waypoints.note: Marshy meadow crossing forces a thigh-high ford of Lemah Creek's braids, followed by roughly 1,000 ft of slide-alder bushwhacking on the meadow's northwest side.
waypoints.directions: An intermittent climbers' path with sparse cairns leads the first thousand feet or so toward Upper Lemah Meadows before fading into open ground. There is no dependable bridge over Lemah Creek, so plan on wading rather than counting on one; the braids run cold and can be thigh-deep, and with high water this is a real obstacle rather than a nuisance.

waypoints.name: Point 3854 cairn line
waypoints.note: Trail fades into brush here; sparse cairns mark the cross-country line where Lemah's five distinct summits and Whinnimic Falls first come into view.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the alder the travel goes straight up the Lemah Creek valley — a mile or two of off-trail ground past small waterfalls and pools, with several more creek crossings and further brushy stretches. Expect wet feet for the rest of the day; there is no line through here that keeps them dry. Most parties camp on a bench in the meadows near 3,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Snow gully and moat transition
waypoints.note: Prominent snow gully gains the east flank; near its top, ~200 ft of wet slabs and running water lead to a moat where snow meets rock — tricky, exposed transition onto the ledges.
waypoints.directions: Carry on up the valley beside the creek to about 5,000 ft, where the snow finger and glacier remnant begin, then take the snow itself: 35-45 degree ground where crampons and an axe are essential and the runout below is bad. Crevasses are few but they are there, so a rope team is worth having across the remnant. Start early enough that the snow is still firm — this is the section that degrades to bare ice and open moats as the snowpack goes.

waypoints.name: Southeast ridge notch
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 ledges gain the notch on the southeast ridge above 7,200 ft; the final summit scramble begins here.

waypoints.name: Lemah Mountain (Main Peak / Lemah Three)
waypoints.note: True summit of the five-tower Lemah massif, first climbed in 1923; last moves are exposed class 3-4 blocks on the summit tower.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency Pass honored in the lot; fill out the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and established shoreline campsites on the north side; the last easy water before the PCT junction.

waypoints.name: PCT Junction near Lemah Meadows
waypoints.note: Pete Lake Trail meets the PCT here; turn north toward Lemah Meadows rather than continuing to Spectacle Lake.

waypoints.name: Avalanche path at Chimney Creek confluence
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT at the first switchback in this avalanche path; a faint, sometimes flagged climber's path drops to a log crossing of the creek and is easy to lose in fog or low light.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Knob
waypoints.note: Standard 2-3 day basecamp on a knob just below the moraine overlooking the falls, roughly 6 hours' hike from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Chimney Glacier bergschrund/moat
waypoints.note: A short pitch of hard ~45-degree glacier ice and a bergschrund/moat crossing guard the base of the East Face; crampons and axe required, and the moat widens as the season progresses.

waypoints.name: Chimney Rock, Main (Central) Summit
waypoints.note: True summit, topped out via 3 pitches of 5.3 rock above the moat; descend via rappels and 3rd-class downclimbing back to the glacier.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency Pass honored in the lot; fill out the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Reached on FR-4616 off Cooper Lake Road, past Cooper Lake.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and established shoreline campsites on the north side; the last easy water before the PCT junction.
waypoints.directions: Roughly four miles of easy, nearly flat forest trail. The tread is in good shape and gets dusty by midsummer, and it is walked fast — none of the day's real work is here.

waypoints.name: PCT Junction near Lemah Meadows
waypoints.note: Pete Lake Trail meets the PCT here; turn north toward Lemah Meadows rather than continuing to Spectacle Lake.
waypoints.directions: Carry on past the lake on the Pete Lake Trail to where it meets the PCT — a short, gentle stretch. Fill up before leaving the lake; above here water means Chimney Creek or melted snow.

waypoints.name: Climber's trail, east side of Chimney Creek
waypoints.note: A climber's path, marked with orange flagging in places, follows the east bank of Chimney Creek up toward Sunrise Knob, staying above the avalanche debris used by the East Face approach.
waypoints.directions: Head north on the PCT about a mile to where it crosses the Chimney Creek avalanche path, and leave the trail there. A logjam gives the creek crossing, and the climber's path starts faint on the far side, running about twenty yards inside the forest alongside the avalanche slope before it firms up. Losing the start puts you in the brush of the avalanche path itself, which is what the flagging is there to prevent.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Knob
waypoints.note: Shared basecamp for both Chimney Rock routes, on a knob just below the moraine overlooking the falls.
waypoints.directions: Steep, brushy climbing up the east bank, crossing several ravines, to the rock buttress at the top. Budget four to five hours from the car to here — the mileage is modest but nearly all the gain and all the route-finding sit in this last stretch.

waypoints.name: Chimney Glacier / moat crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the moat where the upper Chimney Glacier meets the rock; it widens through the season, so look for collapsed snow blocks or a bridge where it narrows.
waypoints.directions: Climb the moraine above camp; a wet, grubby gully through the rock band is the usual way onto the ice, avoiding the icefall. Rope up and cross the upper glacier toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits, keeping clear of the deep bergschrund.

waypoints.name: Notch between the summits
waypoints.note: Roughly three pitches (~600 vertical ft) of wet, slippery ledges and cracks gain this notch between the central and south summits; also used as a rappel/downclimb station on descent.
waypoints.directions: Climb the face to the left of the main gully: about three pitches of wet, slippery fourth-class ground, then a system of ledges, some very wide, to just below the notch. Everything here stays wet, so the short fourth-class steps feel harder than their grade.

waypoints.name: Chimney Rock, South Summit
waypoints.note: South Peak, about 400 vertical feet above the notch; descend by downclimbing the ascent ledges and rappelling the steeper steps.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, continue about 400 ft to the top of the South Peak. This is Chimney Rock's lower south summit, not the central main summit (7,727 ft) that the East Face route climbs. Come down the same way: the ledges are easy to pick out from above, and the steeper sections go with single-rope rappels.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required at the self-issue kiosk; gated Monte Cristo Road begins here and can be hiked or biked.
waypoints.directions: From the Verlot Public Service Center follow the Mountain Loop Highway east about 19.5 miles to the large parking area at Barlow Pass. The highway is paved the whole way now, and the lot fills on summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo Townsite
waypoints.note: Historic ghost-town ruins; do not drink water here or below the site — arsenic from 1890s mine tailings contaminates the soil and creek.
waypoints.directions: Step around the gate and follow the old Monte Cristo mining road east for roughly four miles. It is a wide, nearly flat roadbed with only about 500 ft of gain, so many parties bike it and save an hour in each direction. Expect a washout reroute near the start and a log/footbridge crossing of the South Fork Sauk about a mile in; the road simply ends at the ruins.

waypoints.name: First safe water past the townsite
waypoints.note: Safe drinking water resumes roughly a mile beyond Monte Cristo, once you're clear of the old tailings.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the signed Poodle Dog Pass / Twin Lakes trail behind the townsite and start climbing switchbacks. Carry whatever water you need out of the valley below rather than filling here — it takes about a mile of gain above the site to get clear of the old tailings.

waypoints.name: Poodle Dog Pass
waypoints.note: Trail junction just above Silver Lake — a 0.4 mi spur drops right to Silver Lake while the Twin Lakes Trail climbs left toward the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding the switchbacks, roughly 1,600 ft in about a mile and a half from the townsite, to the signed pass on the ridge.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trail ridge high point
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here (its high point) and head east along the ridge toward Columbia's west spur rather than dropping to Twin Lakes.
waypoints.directions: Ignore the spur dropping right to Silver Lake and take the Twin Lakes Trail left, climbing and contouring along the ridge. It is decently graded but sees less maintenance than the trail below — expect deadfall — and crosses granite slabs higher up. Sunday Creek, about 1.25 miles before Twin Lakes, is the last reliable water on the route; the high point comes before the trail starts losing elevation into the lakes basin.

waypoints.name: SW-face gully below the cliff band
waypoints.note: Wide, loose talus gully with a couple of class 4 moves to enter — notable rockfall hazard, especially with other parties above.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail east onto ledges and talus, crossing the east crest of East Twin Peak, then drop into the boulder fields that fill the 5,300-5,800 ft band. Steep heather benches lead up onto the connecting ridge: stay low on its flank rather than climbing onto the crest, which looks like the line and dead-ends against the upper cliffs. A short 3rd class step gains the wide talus-and-snow field under the cliff band.

waypoints.name: West Chimney crux
waypoints.note: The class 4 chimney regarded as the route's crux: decent footholds but poor handholds; a looser class 3 bypass exists to the right.
waypoints.directions: Keep left of the snow patch that lingers here well into midsummer and work up the loose talus toward the cliff band, then traverse ledges south beneath it around 6,800 ft to find the break. This stretch is where rockfall bites, most of it knocked down by other climbers, so keep the party tight and never directly stacked.

waypoints.name: Columbia Peak
waypoints.note: Hook left/clockwise around the final tower for a short class 3 scramble to the true summit; views of Columbia Glacier, Kyes Peak, and Monte Cristo Peak.
waypoints.directions: Above the break the angle eases back to 3rd class. Follow the west side of the big slabby face over scree-covered slabs, and pass a second short cliff band by a rightward-leaning ramp. A ledge then carries you west and around onto the north side of the tower — crumbly and exposed for a few steps — before the short, solid finish.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Gated old Monte Cristo Road starts here; $5/day or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass required at the self-issue kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Barlow Pass is where the pavement ends on the Mountain Loop Highway. The old Monte Cristo road beyond the gate is closed to cars but open to bikes, and most parties ride it to save their legs for the scramble.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo Townsite
waypoints.note: End of the 4-mile gated gravel road (bike or hike); pick up the Glacier Basin/Glacier Creek trail heading east out of the old mining townsite.
waypoints.directions: Four miles of gently rising gravel road following the South Fork Sauk River. There is a bike rack under the trees at the townsite end; leave the bike there and walk through the old town. Bridges and creek crossings on this stretch have washed out before, so expect the odd detour.

waypoints.name: Ray's Knoll, Glacier Basin
waypoints.note: Timbered knoll in the middle of the basin used as the standard camp; treat water carefully as old mine tailings have contaminated basin runoff with heavy metals.
waypoints.directions: Cross the footbridge on the far side of the townsite and follow signs onto the Glacier Basin Trail, which climbs steadily beside Glacier Creek past a prominent waterfall before easing off into the basin. Aim for the prominent hummock in the middle of the basin. Early in the season the last of this holds patchy snow.

waypoints.name: Erosion gully to headwall waterfall
waypoints.note: Ascend the obvious mine-tailings-colored erosion gully on Cadet's SW face to a headwall with a small waterfall; loose rock underfoot, stay climbers' left of the falls.
waypoints.directions: Find a safe place to ford Glacier Creek — it can be a swift, cold wade during snowmelt — then navigate by the two large boulders: an approximately 15-ft one marks the start of the scramble, and a bigger one across the basin is the next mark. From there start up the reddish blown-out gully, climbing the rib that separates it from the deeper gully immediately to its left. Cairns and occasional flagging carry on where the maintained tread ends.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band crux ledge
waypoints.note: Traverse sharply left on a moderately exposed Class 3 ledge to find the correct notch through the cliff band; easy to lose on the way down.
waypoints.directions: About 25 ft below the waterfall headwall, break out of the gully to climber's left onto a band of red rock. It reads as a dead end from below, and it is the one feature parties lose on the way down — worth building a duck or cairn as you pass through it.

waypoints.name: Southwest ridge crest
waypoints.note: Climber's path exits the brush/scrub onto the ridge crest here; follow heather slopes northeast toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ledges upward through scrub trees and brush, then pick up the faint climbers' path that switchbacks the rest of the way onto the crest.

waypoints.name: Cadet Peak
waypoints.note: True summit register; the subsidiary South Cadet high point is a short detour back along the SW ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest northeast — loose in places, but easy route-finding. Do not be drawn into the deep gully well to climber's left; it is a hazardous false lead. Around 6,500 ft a distinctive hobbit-like rock feature marks a sharp left turn onto a loose talus traverse that runs below the rock and out to the summit ridge. One or two short class 3-4 moves are typical near the top, and everything up here throws rock, so avoid stacking directly below another party.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
