waypoints.note: Gated Monte Cristo Road begins here (open to foot/bike only); Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required at the self-issue kiosk.

waypoints.name: Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail 724 junction / South Fork Sauk River crossing
waypoints.note: Just before the river, the Weden Creek/Gothic Basin trailhead splits off; the Sauk crossing here has no bridge (log crossing only), so many day hikers turn back at this point.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo townsite
waypoints.note: Old mining townsite with an established 6-site Forest Service campground; surface water in the area can contain arsenic and heavy metals from old tailings, so treat or pack water.

waypoints.name: Glacier Falls slick-rock section
waypoints.note: Past the townsite the Glacier Basin Trail turns very steep, climbing wet, slick bedrock alongside Glacier Falls — poor footing, especially descending in the wet.

waypoints.name: Mystery Hill camp (Glacier Basin)
waypoints.note: Established campsites on the timbered knoll of Mystery Hill (site of old Pride of the Mountains/Mystery mine adits) mark the basin high point where the maintained trail effectively ends.

waypoints.name: Dividing ridge / col below the Wilmans Spires
waypoints.note: Leave the basin and climb steep, very loose talus (or snow early season) to the col on the dividing ridge between Glacier Basin and Seventy-Six Basin; loose rock is the main hazard on this section.

waypoints.name: Wilmans Peak (summit)
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 scramble gains the true summit from the dividing ridge; first climbed 1970 via the northwest ridge, with exposed but solid rock on the final pitch.

waypoints.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; road-end parking at the top of FR 2860-120 where a dirt berm blocks further vehicle travel.
waypoints.directions: From US-101 near Sequim, follow Palo Alto Road to Lost Mountain Road (Forest Road 2870), then continue onto Forest Road 2860-120 and drive it to its end. The road stops at a dirt berm that blocks further vehicle travel, at roughly 3,300 feet, where there is room to park. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

waypoints.name: Feeder creek crossing
waypoints.note: Small creek crossing roughly 200 yards below the unmarked trail junction — last reliable water before the dry ridge climb to Baldy.
waypoints.directions: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the road-end berm along an old roadbed and crosses the creek almost straight away. This is the last easy, dependable water for a long stretch, so fill up here before the climb.

waypoints.name: Ridge crest gained
waypoints.note: The climbers' boot path fades and tops out on Gray Wolf Ridge's open crest here; navigation shifts from trail-following to ridge route-finding.
waypoints.directions: Past the crossing the trail narrows to single-track and turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks. In places it is barely a boot-width across eroded, crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale — a climber's path, not a graded trail. It tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short, steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring, the last dependable water on the route.

waypoints.name: Point 6537 (false summit below Baldy)
waypoints.note: Rocky gendarme/false summit marked on maps as Pt. 6537 — Class 2 scramblers typically skirt it on the south side rather than climb straight over.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle turn northwest onto the open ridge crest; navigation shifts from following tread to reading the ridge, so have a map or GPS out. The rocky gendarme ahead is normally skirted on its south side rather than climbed straight over.

waypoints.name: Baldy summit
waypoints.note: True summit of Baldy; the route turns and continues northwest along the open ridge crest toward Gray Wolf Mountain.
waypoints.directions: Rejoin the crest beyond the gendarme — a sign in the saddle marks the Olympic National Park boundary — and walk up the far side to Baldy's top. This stretch is straightforward going on packed dirt and shattered shale, with no scrambling.

waypoints.name: Loose scree/talus saddle
waypoints.note: Steep, loose scree and talus dropping roughly 600 ft off Baldy's north side before Peak 7076 — trekking poles recommended, exposed to wind and fog.
waypoints.directions: From Baldy the route continues northwest and immediately drops about 600 ft off the north side on steep, loose scree and talus, where poles earn their keep. The crest is fully open here and exposed to wind and to fast-moving cloud, so fix the line of the ridge in your mind before committing to the descent.

waypoints.name: Peak '7076' false summit
waypoints.note: Prominent false summit often mistaken for Gray Wolf Mountain from below; the ridge crest continues north over loose talus to the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Climb back out of the saddle and up the crest over loose talus to the prominent bump ahead. Staying close to the ridgeline is generally the cleanest way through the scree. From below this bump reads as the summit, but the crest keeps going north.

waypoints.name: Gray Wolf Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,218 ft), the highest point in Clallam County; views to Vancouver Island, Mt. Olympus, Baker, Rainier, and Glacier Peak.
waypoints.directions: Continue north along the crest over the last of the talus, detouring briefly around the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short class 2-3 scramble on loose rock to the true summit. North-facing gullies on this final stretch can hold steep snow into July.

waypoints.name: Thirtymile Trailhead
waypoints.note: From here, follow Chewuch River Trail #510 to Remmel Lake, then go off-trail south (~2 miles bushwhack) to reach the NW Ridge; this is the line of the 2011 ascent.

waypoints.name: Four Point Lake
waypoints.note: Multiple good campsites with views of Remmel; the usual camp for the Southeast Slope, not on the Remmel Lake approach to this ridge.

waypoints.name: NW Ridge Camp
waypoints.note: Bivy on Remmel's NW Ridge itself, reached by a roughly 2-mile bushwhack south from Remmel Lake.

waypoints.name: Dosewallips Road end (closed-road parking)
waypoints.note: From this road-end, the route continues via bike/foot up West Fork Dosewallips River to Honeymoon Meadows before the Class 2 scramble to White Mountain's summit.

waypoints.name: Dose Forks
waypoints.note: West Fork Dosewallips Trail splits off the main Dosewallips Trail here at the river confluence; reliable water and a designated camp with toilet and bear wires.

waypoints.name: Diamond Meadows Camp
waypoints.note: Last established backcountry camp before Honeymoon Meadows; river-adjacent water source, elevation estimated by interpolating between Dose Forks and Honeymoon Meadows.

waypoints.name: Honeymoon Meadows Camp
waypoints.note: Forested backcountry campsite just below the actual meadows, the standard base camp for the White Mountain scramble day, at about mile 15.

waypoints.name: Anderson Pass
waypoints.note: Divide between the Quinault and Dosewallips drainages and trail junction toward Anderson Glacier; leave the maintained trail here and head south toward White Mountain — little to no water at the pass itself.

waypoints.name: Heather/scree slopes below the summit ridge
waypoints.note: Steep heather and talus that often retains hard, unmarked snow patches into midsummer; carry an ice axe and expect route-finding on this class 2 terrain.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue day-use wilderness permit and NW Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Take Icicle Creek Road to Eightmile Road (FR-7601) and follow it to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and you self-issue a day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk. Worth knowing before you commit to a date: the firm spring snow this route wants, April through June, falls largely before the May 15 to Oct 31 permit season.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and camps; head along the north shore toward the Colchuck Glacier.

waypoints.name: North shore / glacier approach
waypoints.note: Ascend easy snow on the Colchuck Glacier's east lobe toward Colchuck Col.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail; the couloir start is a couple hundred feet left (east) of the col.

waypoints.name: Pandora's Box notch
waypoints.note: Steep snow/ice couloir (up to roughly 35-40 degrees near the bottom) leading to a notch in the ridge; some parties rope up here.

waypoints.name: Dragontail Peak summit
waypoints.note: From the notch, drop down and traverse northeast to the true summit; descend via Aasgard Pass.

waypoints.name: Beverly Turnpike Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-9737-112 off Beverly Creek Road; cross the stout bridge over Beverly Creek right at the trailhead — Northwest Forest Pass required for parking.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road to Beverly Creek Road and follow FR-9737-112 to its end at roughly 3,450-3,600 ft. Wildfire damage has closed this trail system before, so confirm current Forest Service status before committing to the drive in.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek Trail fork
waypoints.note: Beverly Turnpike Trail forks here; leave the Beverly Creek roadbed and turn right (east) up the Bean Creek valley onto Trail #1391.1.
waypoints.directions: Start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed alongside Beverly Creek. At the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the Beverly drainage, which is the wrong valley for this peak.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Bean Creek in a tight, steep valley; can run cold and pushy during June snowmelt, and the trail crosses old avalanche debris just above here.
waypoints.directions: The Bean Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley before dropping to the water. It is an easy rock-hop by mid to late summer, but in May and June snowmelt it runs cold and pushy and is the real decision point of the day; the trail crosses old avalanche debris just above the ford.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek Basin junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks at the edge of subalpine meadows: stay left for Bean Creek Basin's wildflower fields or bear right/east for the Earl Peak saddle approach.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing through forest until it breaks open into the basin — a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. Fill water here. Bean Creek is the last dependable source and there is none above the meadows.

waypoints.name: Earl Pass (southwest ridge gain)
waypoints.note: Saddle on the divide between Bean and Standup Creek drainages; leave the boot path here and gain the southwest ridge toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than continuing left into the upper basin. Tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking up to the broad saddle on the divide, about 2,600 ft of gain in all from the car.

waypoints.name: False summit / loose scree pitch
waypoints.note: Class 1 but exposed to extremely loose, kickable scree on an approximately 70-degree pitch just below the true summit — easy to mistake for the top.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at the pass and pick up the intermittent boot track climbing the ridge directly toward the summit. This is the sustained part of the day: roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting class 2 on loose scree, sand and broken rock, with the track fading in and out. Go slowly, test what you stand on, and stay out from under anyone above.

waypoints.name: Earl Peak summit
waypoints.note: Talus/heather summit block with views across the Teanaway to Mount Stuart; a short ridge scramble continues north to Bean Peak for those extending the trip.
waypoints.directions: From the false top the remaining ground is short — a few more minutes of the same loose ridge tread and talus over the last rise, with no harder moves than what you have already done.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Same start as the East Ridge; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at about road mile 20, elevation roughly 2,100 ft, and park in the trailhead lot. The climb starts by leaving the parking area and backtracking a short way downstream to find a log or a ford across the Cascade River, then picking up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek. This is the same start the East Ridge uses; the trailhead-to-glacier approach is identical for both.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Open-basin camp option after the first two talus fields and a waterfall crossing.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on the flat glacier shelf used to stage the Inspiration/McAllister glacier traverse.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Cross north across Inspiration Glacier to this col, then drop northwest onto the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: McAllister Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Descend the McAllister Glacier toward its southwest gap; navigate visible crevasses, especially late-season.

waypoints.name: Marble Creek–McAllister pass
waypoints.note: Lowest gap on the SW side of the glacier; cross to the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.

waypoints.name: Base of Southwest Buttress gully
waypoints.note: A snow-filled gully roughly 700 vertical feet below the pass leads to the start of the buttress climbing.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: 9-pitch, Grade III, 5.7-5.8 buttress tops out on the true summit after a left-leaning corner on the upper ridge.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Same start as the standard Southwest Buttress; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on the Inspiration Glacier shelf shared with the standard Southwest Buttress route.
waypoints.directions: From the lot, walk about 90 feet back down the road and look for the log or clump of trees spanning the river; cross there, then head roughly 100 feet away from the water to pick up the climbers' path and turn upstream on it. The path climbs steeply through forest and talus into Eldorado Basin and on up to the Inspiration Glacier shelf, about 5,500 ft of gain to camps near 7,400-7,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Crossing point from Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier, shared with the standard buttress approach.
waypoints.directions: Rope up at camp and cross the Inspiration Glacier northeast to the low point on the divide. The ground is otherwise gentle; crevasses are the only real difficulty.

waypoints.name: Marble Creek–McAllister pass
waypoints.note: Shared approach point; the Direct variant departs the standard buttress line higher on the wall, not at the base.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the col onto the McAllister Glacier and work down and across it, keeping to its skier's right where the ice steepens and breaks up, then traverse toward the pass.

waypoints.name: Direct Southwest Buttress topout
waypoints.note: Harder direct start (5.10a) rejoins the standard buttress line before the final corner to the summit ridge.
waypoints.directions: About 700 vertical feet below the pass, start up the prominent gully running to the base of the buttress; it usually holds snow year-round. Rope up before its top, because the moat guarding the base of the rock can open into a deep, exposed gap. From the gully exit do not traverse right onto the standard 1985 line: carry straight on up two direct pitches of 4th and low-5th scrambling to three vertical cracks, take the rightmost at about 5.8 into the strenuous 5.10 crux and mantel onto a large bench, then follow awkward 5.8+ ground toward the large white slabby rock where the original route comes back in.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: True summit shared with the standard Southwest Buttress finish.
waypoints.directions: From the junction with the 1985 line, blocky mid-5th rock and a final corner lead onto the summit ridge, then a short scramble along it gains the true summit.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Standard Eldorado Peak approach start; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road about 20 miles from Marblemount to the large Eldorado Creek trailhead parking area at road mile 20, around 2,100 ft. From the lot, backtrack a short distance downstream to find a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path heading east and upstream on the far bank. This is the shared Eldorado Peak approach, the same start the other Dorado Needle routes use.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Open-basin camp after the first two talus fields, en route to the higher glacier camps.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: High camp on the Inspiration Glacier shelf used for all Eldorado-area and Dorado Needle objectives.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Cross north from Inspiration Glacier over this col onto the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: McAllister Glacier below the gendarmes
waypoints.note: Ascend the McAllister Glacier to just below Dorado Needle's line of gendarmes; this is the start of the NW Ridge, the easiest (1940 first-ascent) line at 5.4.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: Three pitches of class 5.4 rock past the gendarmes gain the true summit.

waypoints.name: Northwest Ridge approach point (NW of Dorado Needle)
Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)
waypoints.note: Old overgrown roadbed departs SR 20 here paralleling Goodell Creek; NOCA backcountry permit (from the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center) required for any overnight.
waypoints.directions: From SR-20 near Newhalem, turn off just east of Goodell Creek Campground to reach the Goodell Creek Upper Group Campground trailhead, at about 600 feet, where the old overgrown roadbed departs the highway paralleling Goodell Creek. The unsigned climbers' path itself starts behind a large boulder near the campground. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, available from the Marblemount Wilderness Info Center, is required for any overnight.

waypoints.name: Stone-arrow/cairn turnoff to Terror Basin path
waypoints.note: A stone arrow/large cairn at the end of the old Goodell Creek roadbed marks the unsigned turnoff onto the boot path climbing toward Terror Basin; easy to walk past.
waypoints.directions: Pick the path up on the east side of Goodell Creek — it starts behind a large boulder near the campground, not at the campground sign on the west bank — then follow the old roadbed up the valley at a gentle grade. It is unmaintained: dozens of downed logs and a couple of washouts make these four miles far slower than the profile suggests, so budget two to four hours rather than judging pace by the mileage.

waypoints.name: Last water before the hill climb
waypoints.note: No reliable water again until Terror Basin, so tank up here before the steep 4,000 ft climb begins.
waypoints.directions: The boot path leaves the end of the roadbed and enters the trees, gaining only a hundred feet or so before reaching this crossing. It is a few minutes' walk, and the last flat ground before the climbing starts in earnest.

waypoints.name: Treeline / heather benches
waypoints.note: Boot-beaten path gains roughly 4,000 ft in 2 miles (steeper than the old Mailbox Peak trail) before breaking out of forest onto open heather and rock benches.
waypoints.directions: From here the path turns straight uphill and gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles on a steep, unrelenting boot track with more blowdown to duck. Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, swings left, and makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band around 4,800 ft before kicking up one last steep gully onto open ground.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin camp
waypoints.note: Gravelly wildflower basin with several small streams; the established tent sites here are the standard base camp, a long day's carry from the trailhead (6-8 hours with overnight packs).
waypoints.directions: Heather benches and granite slabs lead north for a couple of miles to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft, the high point of the whole approach. The north side of that notch is the crux of getting in, not the climb: about 400 vertical feet of steep, loose choss when it is melted out — stay skier's-right, as going straight down is a bad idea — or a firmer snow finger when it is filled in, capped by a short steep headwall that some parties rope up for or protect with a lower.

waypoints.name: Terror Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Short, low-angle crossing of the Terror Glacier remnant above the glacial lake outlet, reached over benches and granite slabs from camp; most parties go unroped with crampons in stable conditions, but it can show bare ice late in the season and is not crevasse-free.

waypoints.name: 7,200 ft Inspiration-McMillan col
waypoints.note: Top of the steep snow and rock gully above the Terror Glacier, between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire — the same col used again on the downclimb.
waypoints.directions: From the Terror Glacier, climb the snow and rock gully, which steepens to roughly 40 degrees near the top, to the col on the west ridge — the same col you will use again on the downclimb.

waypoints.name: West McMillan Spire summit
waypoints.note: True summit of West McMillan Spire (Grade II, 4th class on the west ridge); exposed final scrambling moves.
waypoints.directions: Above the col the ridge relaxes into a long scramble on scree, heather and broken rock, with a choice between more solid rock steps and looser talus. There is no sustained difficulty, but the footing is poor enough to make it slow in both directions, and rockfall onto a party strung out below is the main hazard here — keep the group tight. A short, exposed step gains the summit block: it starts loose and scree-covered before the rock improves markedly near the top, and the exposure concentrates in the last few moves between the false summit and the true one, where the crest narrows and drops away on both sides. Some parties fix a hand line for that stretch.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (#96)
waypoints.note: Trail 96 begins here on FR 2150; Northwest Forest Pass required and self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 2150, at about 4,600 feet, where the Snowgrass Flat Trail (#96) begins. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and a free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit is available at the trailhead kiosk. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm current conditions before driving in.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flats meadows
waypoints.note: Trail 96 opens into heather meadows and wildflower bogs with reliable creek water; camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself per Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)) — use designated sites above/below the flats instead. Trail 86 splits here toward Goat Lake.

waypoints.name: Trail 97 junction
waypoints.note: Trail 97, the bypass trail, forks west here toward Cispus Basin; stay on Trail 96, which continues up through the meadows to the PCT.

waypoints.name: PCT junction
waypoints.note: Trail 96 tops out on the Pacific Crest Trail; turn north and climb a series of open benches with views of Mt. Adams and the Goat Rocks crest.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy climbers'-path junction
waypoints.note: Unmarked junction where an unmaintained climbers' path leaves the PCT for Old Snowy; many parties stash trekking poles/packs here before the scramble.

waypoints.name: Summit scree/talus scramble
waypoints.note: Final ~0.5 mi/350 ft leaves the tread for loose scree and talus with a short Class 3 hand-climbing section; watch for rockfall dislodged by climbers above and lingering steep snow into early summer.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit (7,880+ ft); panoramic views of Mt. Adams, Mt. Rainier, Mt. St. Helens and the McCall, Conrad and Meade Glaciers, with Packwood Glacier visible just below to the northwest.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large parking lot on SR 20 just east of milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass. The trail follows Canyon Creek about 6 miles to the Mill Creek Trail junction, the start of this route's approach. The east-side line up the East Ridge starts elsewhere, at a locked gate on the Slate Creek road below Harts Pass (about 3,800 ft).

waypoints.name: Mill Creek ford
waypoints.note: Ford Mill Creek just below the trail junction — last reliable, easy-to-reach water before the long climb toward Azurite.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Canyon Creek tread here and turn up the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail; maintained trail effectively ends beyond this point.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Mill Creek Trail
waypoints.note: Tread disappears under heavy slide alder and downed timber left from the mine-era trail's disuse — expect a slow, scratchy alder-hacking bushwhack for several miles.

waypoints.name: Azurite Mine
waypoints.note: Flat ground amid the old defunct copper/silver mine workings on Mill Creek; the common overnight camp before pushing toward the Ballard basin.

waypoints.name: Azurite–Ballard basin
waypoints.note: Reached via roughly 3 more brush-choked miles above the mine; open basin at the base of Ballard's south slopes and a typical bivy before the summit push.

waypoints.name: South-face brush and gully route-finding
waypoints.note: Steep, loose terrain with several look-alike chutes low on the south face — picking the wrong gully here is the main way parties get cliffed out or turned back.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; parking lot is just past the Downey Creek bridge on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), about 20 mi from Hwy 530.
waypoints.directions: Drive Suiattle River Road (FR 26) about 20 miles in from Highway 530; the parking area sits just past the Downey Creek bridge at roughly 1,450 feet. Display a Northwest Forest Pass. Check the road before you commit to the trip, because it is frequently washed out or gated well short of the trailhead, adding miles of walking or biking each way that none of the trail mileage here accounts for. The route is normally in condition July through September.

waypoints.name: Sixmile Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp along the easy, flat Downey Creek Trail #768 where the route leaves the maintained trail and turns east along Bachelor Creek.
waypoints.directions: Follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles from the trailhead — easy, well-graded and mostly flat through forest, with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford or log-cross Bachelor Creek to its south side here; the climbers' path above is badly overgrown with slide alder up to roughly 4,400 ft.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends here; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first, then ford to the south side at about the 9.5-mile mark. Treat it as a real creek crossing — harder and more dangerous in high water or early season.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake Pass
waypoints.note: Gap on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake (~5,880 ft), gained by switchbacks; begin the ~500 ft descent to the lake basin from here.
waypoints.directions: Climb the climbers' path above the crossing. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone, so expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber; above the debris the path climbs to the pass on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake
waypoints.note: High camp with reliable water at the lake basin; Itswoot Ridge, reached by traversing further, is the alternate camp some parties use instead.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 500 ft off the pass into the lake basin. These are snow slopes into midsummer and this is normally the crux navigation of the approach day when they are covered.

waypoints.name: Dome Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the Dome Glacier's crevasses toward the Dome-Sinister col; a bergschrund spans the glacier and requires finding a solid snowbridge.
waypoints.directions: Most parties push on from the lake basin up onto Itswoot Ridge for high camp, then traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the glacier. Rope up for glacier travel and carry crevasse-rescue gear before starting across.

waypoints.name: Dome-Sinister col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Dome and Sinister Peaks; from here contour on an easy snowfield around to Sinister's south side to reach the loose southwest gully.
waypoints.directions: Cross over the Dome–Chikamin col and descend the crevassed Chikamin Glacier to about 7,200 ft, then traverse right (east) across the glacier to the col. The bergschrund guarding it can be hard to cross in late season and has sometimes required a short rappel to get down onto or across it.

waypoints.name: Sinister Peak
waypoints.note: True summit, just under a mile east of Dome Peak along the connecting ridge; reached via the loose southwest gully to the upper west ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the col contour around on an easy snowfield to Sinister's south side, then climb the loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge and scramble Class 2–3 along the ridge to the top. Loose rock in the gully is the main hazard — move fast and keep the party out of each other's fall line; some parties skip it and take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trail 768 starts here; FR 26 (Suiattle River Rd) is washed out ~4.5 mi below the trailhead (closed through at least 2028), so expect a 15-16 mi road walk/bike just to reach this point. Vault toilet only, no potable water; day-use pass required.
waypoints.directions: From Darrington, take the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) east toward the trailhead. Check the current closure point before you go and build the extra road miles into the schedule — bikes are the usual answer to them. A day-use pass is required, and there is no potable water at the road end.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Creek Trail junction & crossing
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Downey Creek Trail for the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path; ford or log-cross Bachelor Creek here — logs are slick, use a pole for balance.
waypoints.directions: Follow Downey Creek Trail #768 up the valley on the east bank at a gentle grade through old-growth. The tread is rough and lightly maintained — brush, blowdown and washed-out sections — and past avalanche cycles have swept debris across the valley and buried stretches of it. The junction is unsigned and easy to walk straight past, so start watching for it around the six-mile mark.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Meadows
waypoints.note: Open subalpine meadow camp near timberline; tread beyond this point is faint, brushy, and easy to lose in fog.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the creek the climbers' path turns steeply uphill through brush, avalanche debris and old timber, climbing out of the valley toward timberline. It crosses open avalanche paths below Spire Point on the way, which are worth assessing for stability if there is still snow sitting on them.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake
waypoints.note: Cross the ~5,880 ft gap northwest of the lake, then drop to Cub Lake's basin — reliable water and a common base camp for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Climb east through heather benches and boulder terrain to the gap on the ridge, then take the steep 500 ft drop into the lake basin on its far side. Talus and brush make this stretch hard to follow in cloud — hold a line you can see rather than casting about for tread that is not there.

waypoints.name: Itswoot Ridge camp
waypoints.note: Established ridge camp with running water nearby, close to Itswoot Lake (~5,020 ft) just below; last reliable camp before the glacier.
waypoints.directions: A climbers' trail switchbacks up out of the lake basin onto the ridge above; allow about an hour from the lake. It costs 900 ft with a full pack but takes that hour off the start of summit day.

waypoints.name: Dome Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up here — the glacier is actively crevassed; pick a line around visible crevasses toward the notch below the summit pyramid.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp early. A boot path crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, then the route drops about 200 ft and traverses cross-country on roughly an 80 degree bearing below the cliff bands, over glacier-polished slabs — bare rock late in the season, snow-covered early — and a boulder-and-snow slope to the glacier's toe. This is about two miles across the Spire Creek cirque with nothing marked, on exposed and sometimes loose ground, so carry a map and compass or a GPS track.

waypoints.name: Notch below summit pyramid
waypoints.note: Gain this notch just north of the true summit before the final rock arete and short snow slope.
waypoints.directions: Travel roped on roughly a 115 degree bearing up-glacier, working through the visible crevasse bands. A bergschrund below the notch is the step that most often needs a rappel on the way down, so look at how open it is on the way up and note what you could build an anchor from — there is nothing fixed anywhere on this route.

waypoints.name: Dome Peak
waypoints.note: True (northeast) summit of Dome Peak's twin-summit ridge; first climbed by George Freed and Eric Larson in 1936.
waypoints.directions: A short snow slope of about 300 ft gains the summit ridge east of the true summit, then roughly 500 ft of narrow, exposed Class 4 arete leads to the top. The crux is a straddled cheval move between the two summit horns, which many parties sling or protect with a handline. The rock is largely featureless, so work out the protection on the way up: this is the section people belay coming back down.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start point for the 2-day approach (Hannegan Pass -> Easy Ridge -> Pickell Pass) used on this route's first ascent.
waypoints.directions: Drive Forest Road 32, the Hannegan Pass Road, to its end at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,120 ft. The road is normally open to the trailhead through summer and early fall but has a documented history of washout damage needing bypass construction, so confirm current status with the Glacier Public Service Center before driving in. Park with a Northwest Forest or interagency pass displayed; the overnight wilderness permit for everything past Hannegan Pass is a separate Park Service permit picked up in Glacier or Marblemount.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail (#674); stay on the maintained trail here and descend into the Chilliwack valley; the cross-country toward Easy Ridge starts far below, after the river ford, and the Copper Ridge trail branches down in the valley rather than at the pass.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley, about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to the 5,050 ft pass, with Mount Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge across the valley. The grade is gentle and the tread is good the whole way, and the Ruth Creek crossings in the first couple of miles carry reliable water.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River ford
waypoints.note: Ford the Chilliwack River below Easy Ridge on the climbers' path past Copper Creek before switchbacking back up; can be a cold, thigh-deep crossing in early season.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the maintained trail keeps going, and this is the stretch people get wrong: do not leave it here. Descend the switchbacks north-east into the Chilliwack valley, losing about 1,500 ft over roughly three miles to the Copper Creek area at a little over 3,000 ft, where the Copper Ridge trail branches away and is not your turn. Continue past it on the climbers' path and drop to the Chilliwack River ford below Easy Ridge. The crossing is cold and can run thigh-deep in early season, so pick a braided section, unclip your hipbelt, and cross before the afternoon melt comes down. The climbers' path switchbacks straight back up the far side, so this low point at about 2,750 ft is the bottom of the whole approach.

waypoints.name: Bivy beyond Easy Peak
waypoints.note: Established climbers' bivy near the summit of Easy Peak (6,613'), reached via the Easy Ridge climbers' path that climbs from the Chilliwack River ford; typical end of day one.
waypoints.directions: From the river, switchback steeply back up onto Easy Ridge and then follow the crest itself. This is a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge with almost no shade; flowing water shows up relatively early along it, but the first-ascent party warned this stretch would be brutal later in the season and in dry years, so fill up while you can. Continue along and over Easy Peak to the established bivy beyond it, roughly a ten-hour day with a full pack from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Imperfect Impasse
waypoints.note: A notch on Easy Ridge that must be downclimbed and re-ascended to continue toward the Pickets proper; exposed and slower than it looks from a distance.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp and keep going along the ridge off-trail toward the Pickets, dropping to the cleft known as the Imperfect Impasse. This leg is route-finding and exposed scrambling rather than walking, and the notch has to be downclimbed and then re-ascended on the far side; parties consistently find it slower than it looks from a distance.

waypoints.name: Challenger Col
waypoints.note: Snow/glacier col that gains the western slope of the range; parties have noted a bergschrund forming near its top by mid-to-late season.
waypoints.directions: Out of the notch, regain elevation onto the flank of Mount Challenger and climb through Challenger Col. This is snow and glacier ground rather than rock, so rope up and treat it as crevassed terrain; parties have reported a bergschrund opening near the top of the col by mid to late season.

waypoints.name: Pickle Pass
waypoints.note: Gap below Spectre's serrated south ridge of hoodoos, visible from Frenzel Camp, where the technical climbing on the route begins.
waypoints.directions: From the col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, staying roped near the pocket glacier. Phantom's west and south ridge is the usual second bivy and where most parties stop for the night. Pickle Pass itself can hold snow well into the season, and the first-ascent party found it snowed over and skirted it rather than crossing.

waypoints.name: Spectre Peak
waypoints.directions: From the base of the south ridge, start up right of the entry notch: about 100 ft of fourth class leads into blocky 5.7 climbing, then low-fifth ground to a large tree-dotted ledge and a traverse left onto the crest proper. The crest gives sustained 5.4 to 5.8 climbing past the crux third pitch, a short overhanging band of 5.9 choss above sparse gear on the face right of a mossy gully, and past a shattered gendarme at pitch 7 where a 25 m rappel into the gap is followed by a self-belayed ascent of the far wall. The last pitch weaves through narrow, chalky hoodoo towers to a 30 m rappel off the final tower onto a big grassy ledge, from which about 600 ft of third and fourth class with a couple of low-fifth moves leads to the top.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FS Road 32; Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk — standard access point for Mount Challenger/Picket Range approaches via Hannegan Pass Trail #674.
waypoints.directions: Drive Forest Road 32 to its end, where the Hannegan Pass Trailhead sits at about 3,120 ft and Trail #674 starts. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and there is a kiosk at the parking area. Plan the trip for July through September, once the Hannegan Pass road is snow-free and the Challenger Glacier crevasses are more consolidated. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required for the Perfect Pass zone, which is walk-up only and cannot be reserved ahead.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail ends at the pass crest; leave it here and drop east into the Chilliwack River valley to pick up the unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' path toward Perfect Pass.

waypoints.name: Imperfect Impasse (Easy Ridge)
waypoints.note: Steep, often wet and slippery down-climbing slabs above a deep gorge on Easy Ridge — the cross-country crux of the approach and a common turnaround point in poor conditions.

waypoints.name: Perfect Pass
waypoints.note: Established high bivy on the ridge crest between Easy Ridge and Mount Challenger; the standard base camp for Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle climbs (alternative to a Luna Cirque camp).

waypoints.name: Challenger Arm gap
waypoints.note: Traverse around Challenger Arm to gain the edge of the Challenger Glacier; rope up for glacier travel here.

waypoints.name: Challenger Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Roped travel across open crevasses on the Challenger Glacier; the well-trodden track runs roughly 3 miles from Perfect Pass/Challenger Arm to the base of Poltergeist Pinnacle.

waypoints.name: Base of Poltergeist Pinnacle (East Face dihedral)
waypoints.note: Leave the glacier at the pinnacle's base; the East Face route starts in a short technical dihedral system just left of the dike-streaked shield feature.

waypoints.name: Poltergeist Pinnacle
waypoints.note: Small, exposed summit block on the southernmost of the subsidiary pinnacles between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb; the way down continues along the ridge to Mount Challenger's summit and down its glacier route, not back down the face.

waypoints.name: Monument Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; no water/restrooms on-site; trail 484 starts off FR 5400 near the end of Lost River Road.

waypoints.name: Eureka Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Footlog/ford where the old bridge has repeatedly washed out; last reliable water for the next ~8 miles and 5,000 ft of climbing up Pistol Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Trail 484 runs north up the Lost River valley for about four miles of easy walking — the only maintained stretch of trail on the whole trip. The unbridged crossing is the one real hazard on this leg: during June and early-July runoff it can run thigh- to waist-deep, so cross in the cool of the morning when flows are lowest and be prepared to turn around rather than force it.

waypoints.name: Abandoned Pistol Ridge trail split
waypoints.note: Maintained tread ends at Eureka Creek; from here the route follows the old, unmaintained Pistol Pass trail steeply onto the crest of Pistol Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Fill every bottle at the creek — there is no reliable water from here until the lake basin, roughly eight miles and 5,000 ft of climbing away. Beyond the crossing the tread degrades into an abandoned trail climbing steeply out of the valley, with heavy deadfall, brush, and stretches where the path disappears entirely and cairns are all you have to follow.

waypoints.name: Pistol Ridge crest side-hill
waypoints.note: Exposed, poorly-defined tread along the ridge crest with steep drop-offs; easy to lose the path in fog or early-season snow.
waypoints.directions: Climb steeply onto the ridge crest, about 1,800 ft over two and a half miles on faint, unmaintained tread. Expect to lose the path repeatedly in blowdown and brush and to navigate by cairn and map rather than by tread.

waypoints.name: Pistol Pass
waypoints.note: High saddle on Pistol Ridge marking the top of the approach; from here the route drops off-trail toward Lake of the Woods and Monument-Lake basin.
waypoints.directions: Continue along the crest to the saddle, another 900 ft of gain spread over roughly three miles, picking up cairns where the tread fades out. This tops out the approach climb — from the creek ford it is about 5,000 ft of gain, all of it dry.

waypoints.name: Lake of the Woods
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake between Lake and Pistol Peaks with several established campsites; primary water source and base camp for the summit day.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and follow the basin about a mile north past the lake to the established camps. This is the first water since the creek ford. Parties commonly arrive here after dark at the end of a nine-hour-plus day, so know where the camps sit before you get close.

waypoints.name: Lake Mountain east ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Leave camp and gain Lake Mountain's east ridge directly above the lake basin; loose but solid granite, Class 2-3 with some exposure.
waypoints.directions: From camp, climb northwest straight out of the lake basin through the larches toward the lower east ridge. Do not try to go straight up the peak's south side — a subsidiary rock knob (Point 8165) and a cliff band near 8,000 ft bar a direct line, which is why the route swings around to the east ridge. All of this is off-trail talus, scree, and boulder-field travel.

waypoints.name: Lake Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit; broad, rocky top with views across the Pasayten toward Monument Peak and the Lost River drainage.
waypoints.directions: Follow the east ridge over blocky granite through larches and boulder fields, mostly Class 2 with occasional exposed Class 2-3 moves. Where the summit ridge meets the southeast slopes there is a short, roughly half-pitch stretch of genuinely exposed Class 3 that reads harder downclimbing than climbing, so note your line as you pass it. Stay on the crest or its south side and well clear of the north wall and northeast face, which are much steeper and not part of this route.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead (Cross-Country Zone Access, Upper Goodell Creek)
waypoints.note: Goodell Creek Trail -> Terror Creek ford -> The Barrier -> Crescent Creek Basin -> Eye Col approach used for all Twin Needles routes.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek logjam crossing
waypoints.note: Climbers' path fades to bushwhack here; cross Terror Creek by fording, or on a big log just upstream when one is in place (last reliable water before the steep, cliffy push up toward the Barrier).

waypoints.name: The Barrier ridge crossing
waypoints.note: Loose, exposed scrambling (harder late-season without snow cover) gains this ridge that separates the Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek Basin.

waypoints.name: Chopping Block saddle camp (above Crescent Creek Basin)
waypoints.note: Established bivy sites on the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block, used as base camp for both Twin Needles; Crescent Creek Basin, the talus/scree basin below the south-facing summit gullies, lies about 200 ft below.

waypoints.name: Eye Col
waypoints.note: Class-5 chockstone squeeze gains the notch between the summit gullies shared with West Twin Needle; rope up for this section.

waypoints.name: East Twin Needle
waypoints.note: East Twin Needle sits atop 'Eye Col' immediately adjacent to West Twin Needle.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard access point via FR-56/Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road; no day-use fee is currently charged at this specific trailhead (per USFS), though a free self-issue wilderness permit is required beyond it for Alpine Lakes Wilderness travel, and the road washout beyond this point means biking or hiking the closed roadbed toward Dutch Miller Gap.
waypoints.directions: FR-56 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to the lot is heavily potholed and rutted; parties in low-clearance cars routinely park short and walk the last stretch, which adds to an already long day.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Lake
waypoints.note: Standard high camp for the route, roughly 10 mi in via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail/old roadbed then a steep, unmaintained forested slog above a river ford near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trail; seldom-visited alpine lake below the Overcoat Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: The continuation of the road past the gate is roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed to Hardscrabble Horse Camp, and most parties bike it rather than walk it. Beyond that the Dutch Miller Gap Trail runs east along the north bank; the tread is reasonable but summer thimbleberry buries the rocks underfoot. Leave the trail about a mile before it swings toward Williams Lake and ford the river: it can run thigh-to-waist deep, and it is colder and higher on the way back than it was in the morning.

waypoints.name: Rock benches above Overcoat Glacier
waypoints.note: Higher alternate camp on open benches used to shorten summit day; this bivy option sits at roughly 6,600 ft.
waypoints.directions: Above the ford the ground climbs steeply through brush into a rocky corridor of waterfalls and steep faces before opening onto snow and benches. Snow lingers here well past midsummer. The awkward part is a sloping rock step partway up, which is markedly harder to downclimb than to climb and is worth noting for the return.

waypoints.name: Notch on Overcoat Peak's north ridge (Overcoat Col)
waypoints.note: Contour east from camp to this notch to gain the upper Overcoat Glacier; a col of the same name and elevation (~6,800 ft) sits beneath Chimney Rock's east face.
waypoints.directions: Only a couple of hundred feet of net gain, but it is a rising traverse over benches and old snow rather than a walk. The glacier starts immediately on the far side, so rope up and fit crampons at the notch rather than after stepping onto it.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier's lower snowfields toward the snow finger below the east face; expect deep crevasses and weak, undermined snow bridges on this rapidly retreating glacier.
waypoints.directions: Drop onto the upper glacier from the notch and work toward the snow finger below the east face. Most parties time this route for the tail end of summer, when the crevasses are open and visible and the rock above is clear of snow; earlier in the season the bridges are the thing that will catch you out.

waypoints.name: Snow finger to east face
waypoints.note: Find the snow finger leading off the glacier onto the east face here, then pick up the Class 3-4 ledges and steep gully toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: The finger rises off the top of the glacier and is steep enough that crampons and a second tool are the norm. A crevasse commonly cuts it partway up and has to be turned. Near the dark towers at its top, move off snow onto rock and round the corner east to reach the ledge system.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; the final ~400 vertical ft is Class 4/low-5.0 ledges and a steep gully on the east side, with a small summit register.
waypoints.directions: The gully has solid holds but a few tall steps force committing, exposed moves, and most parties pitch it out on small cams and nuts in mediocre rock rather than soloing it. Sort the descent before you commit: the damp dihedral below is normally rappelled twice, not downclimbed.

waypoints.name: Westside Road / Dry Creek (Tahoma Creek) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of driveable Westside Road (3.2 mi from the Nisqually-Longmire Rd junction), gated at Dry Creek. Check this before you drive: the National Park Service's only two listed accesses to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground — the next waypoint on this route — are Kautz Creek (11.5 mi round trip) and Longmire (13 mi round trip). The Westside Road and Tahoma Creek corridor is not among them, and route beta for Success Cleaver reports the Tahoma Creek Trail closed for flood hazard, leaving Longmire via the Wonderland Trail as the standard approach. The mileages recorded on this route's waypoints are measured from this Dry Creek gate, so they describe the older corridor rather than a Longmire or Kautz Creek start — treat them as approximate if you approach from either of those, and confirm current trail status with a wilderness information centre.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the park's south-west corner; the road is paved and open essentially year round, conditions permitting. Westside Road leaves the Nisqually to Longmire road and is driveable about three miles to the gate at Dry Creek, where a standing, non-seasonal closure caused by repeated Tahoma Creek washouts stops vehicles; past the gate it is open to foot and bike traffic only. Longmire, where the nearest wilderness information centre is and where you register in and out, lies about 3.5 miles further along the main road.

waypoints.name: Indian Henry's Hunting Ground (patrol cabin)
waypoints.note: Historic 1915 patrol cabin marks where the route leaves the maintained Wonderland Trail for cross-country travel toward the Mirror Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Mirror Lakes
waypoints.note: Small tarns about a mile off the Wonderland Trail; last dependable water before contouring dry southwest/west slopes of Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained Wonderland Trail at the patrol cabin and take the Mirror Lakes spur west, crossing marshy meadow on a series of plank walkways. Maintained tread ends part way along and the path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft, in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak, roughly a mile off the Wonderland. These tarns are the last dependable water before the dry south-west and west slopes of Pyramid Peak.

waypoints.name: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
waypoints.note: Flat campsites just north of this 6,631 ft high point give broad views of Success Cleaver; position is estimated, not surveyed — interpolated along the contour around Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: From the tarns it is cross-country travel. Head north-east out of the basin and contour the south-west then west slopes of Pyramid Peak, staying roughly between 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. There is no boot-pack and only sparse cairning through here, so carry a map or GPS track and expect to find your own line; snowmelt water is often available around the point into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak near 6,300 ft is a common first night.

waypoints.name: 6,400 ft saddle below Success Cleaver
waypoints.note: Short descent NNE from Point 6631 to this saddle; typical high camp before scrambling onto the lower cleaver at first light.
waypoints.directions: Drop north-north-east from Point 6631 a short way to the saddle at about 6,400 ft, which is the start of Success Cleaver proper. It is a scree and loose-boulder col and it looks unpleasant, which is how you know it is the right place. There is an easier way down into it than the obvious line, and parties record missing it and taking the worst ground, so pick the descent out before you commit and note it for the return.

waypoints.name: Lower Success Cleaver gendarmes
waypoints.note: Loose rock towers force weaving route-finding on the lower rib; rockfall risk climbs if other parties are above; bivy options around 8,100-8,300 ft.
waypoints.directions: From the col the cleaver rises straight ahead and does not let up: loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, no track and no cairned line, weaving among rock towers on ground you route-find yourself. Use what is on either side as the test. The South Tahoma Glacier should fall away to climber's left and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to climber's right; if you find yourself on a glacier, or if the going out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you have drifted off the cleaver and are contouring around Pyramid Peak instead. Rockfall risk rises sharply with any party above you, the rock firms up above roughly 7,000 ft, and there are bivy sites around 8,100 to 8,300 ft.

waypoints.name: Rockfall chutes to Kautz Cleaver headwall
waypoints.note: Angle across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall and gain the Kautz Cleaver near 12,600 ft; helmet mandatory, best crossed before sun loosens rock.
waypoints.directions: Follow the cleaver crest up through class 3 and short class 4 rock bands and steep chutes, past bivy benches near 9,400 ft and the small col at about 10,700 ft. Higher, the crest holds a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow has melted off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies and across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall, joining the Kautz Cleaver between roughly 12,200 and 12,600 ft. Cross those chutes early, before the sun starts releasing rock and ice; helmets on.

waypoints.name: Point Success
waypoints.directions: From the Kautz Cleaver climb steepening snow and ice, generally around 45 degrees, to the headwall below the summit. A cliff band bars the way and is passed either by a short low fifth class rock step, exposed and sometimes wet or icy, or by an isolated snow and ice pitch of about 15 ft at up to 55 degrees, depending on the season. Above it the angle eases onto the summit plateau at Point Success, 14,158 ft.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin Pullout
waypoints.note: Large paved pullout at the hairpin turn on the North Cascades Highway just east of Washington Pass crest; no signed trailhead — find the boot path into the timber/boulder field on the uphill side. No parking pass is needed at this highway turnout.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the first hairpin turn about a mile east of the Washington Pass summit and park in the large paved turnout on the south side of the road, around 5,160 ft. Nothing here is signed as a trailhead; the boot path starts on the uphill side of the pullout, into the timber and boulders. SR-20 is gated for winter from roughly early December to mid or late April, so check the WSDOT pass report in the shoulder seasons. No parking pass is needed at this highway turnout.

waypoints.name: Boulder Field / Snowline
waypoints.note: Cairns mark the climbers' path up through timber and talus to about 5,800 ft, where the route commonly meets lingering snowpack well into summer.
waypoints.directions: From the pullout head south and southeast toward the foot of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch, below the north side of Kangaroo Temple. Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus and follow the cairns carefully: this lower boulder and talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach, and it is considerably worse when snow covers the tread early in the season. Around 5,800 ft you reach the level where snowpack commonly lingers well into summer.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Gain the crest of Kangaroo Ridge here between Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, about 1,500 ft above the trailhead; leave the approach path and turn east onto Wallaby's southwest ridge.
waypoints.directions: Above the boulder band the tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail through the upper basin. Keep climbing mixed talus, boulders and open slope to the crest of Kangaroo Ridge at Kangaroo Pass, 6,671 ft, roughly 1,500 ft of gain from the car in about 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only water on the route and can be dry by late summer or fall; there is none higher, so carry enough from the car. Expect snow on this stretch into early or mid summer depending on the year, and carry an ice axe or microspikes into July.

waypoints.name: 7,400 ft Ridge-to-Face Swing
waypoints.note: The southwest ridge narrows here; step off the crest and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully — boot tracks are sparse and easy to lose in poor visibility.
waypoints.directions: Leave the boot path at the pass and gain Wallaby's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail runs a short way and then disappears on rock, so the rest is route-finding: stay on or near the crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree and grassy benches, about 530 ft of gain to an access notch near 7,200 ft. The short section between that notch and about 7,400 ft is the technical crux of the route and holds a corniced snow arete into late spring, where an axe and light crampons are commonly used.

waypoints.name: South-Facing Summit Gully
waypoints.note: Loose talus and scree gully gains the final several hundred feet; Class 3 rock on either side avoids the worst scree, and this same gully is the descent line — watch for rockfall from parties above.
waypoints.directions: Where the crest narrows near 7,400 ft, step off it and traverse onto the south-facing flank to reach the summit gully. Boot tracks are sparse here and easy to lose in poor visibility. The gully is moderately steep with a great deal of loose rock and scree, so wear a helmet and avoid stacking the party directly above one another, since anyone higher will kick debris onto anyone below. Many parties take a short Class 3 line on the more solid rock at the gully's margins rather than wading up the scree.

waypoints.name: Wallaby Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Wallaby Peak on Kangaroo Ridge (7,995 ft); first climbed by Fred and Helmy Beckey with Walt Varney on June 17, 1942.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully for the final several hundred feet, then near its top exit left, to the northeast, for the short scramble to the true summit at 7,995 ft. The slabs just below the summit block stay exposed and are genuinely committing when wet or snow-covered, even in midsummer. This same gully is the descent line, downclimbed one at a time.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Lake / Yellow Aster Butte Trailhead
waypoints.note: On FR 3065 (Twin Lakes Road), 4.5 mi up from SR 542, where the road continues about 2 rough miles to Twin Lakes; Northwest Forest Pass required and roadside parking along the switchbacks is very limited.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Signed fork below Gold Run Pass: right climbs over the pass and drops to Tomyhoi Lake, route stays left toward Yellow Aster Butte meadows.
waypoints.directions: Start on the Yellow Aster Butte trail and climb steeply — roughly 1,500 ft in the first mile and a half — through an avalanche path and then forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal creeks low down that are the easiest water on the route early in the season. At the signed fork the right branch carries on over the pass and down to Tomyhoi Lake; stay left for the Yellow Aster meadows.

waypoints.name: Yellow Aster tarns / meadows
waypoints.note: High plateau of small glacier-carved tarns; all camping must be at or beyond this point (LNT-only, camp on snow/rock/bare ground, not the fragile meadow turf) — reliable water from the tarns.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the fork the grade eases and the trail traverses the south flank of the butte for a bit over two miles as the terrain opens into meadow. At an unsigned junction around three and a half miles the path to the butte's summit goes right; drop left instead on narrow, steep switchbacks into the tarn basin.

waypoints.name: Boot path onto Tomyhoi Arm
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the well-defined climbers' boot path heading north along the crest of Tomyhoi Arm toward the southeast ridge.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the basin and head north-northwest, over a broad hump and down to a col near 6,270 ft, where a well-beaten climbers' boot path picks up along the crest. Getting onto the right crest is the thing to be careful about here — the arm runs north toward the peak, and the trail system does not go that way.

waypoints.name: Moat below Tomyhoi Glacier remnant
waypoints.note: Shallow moat/hard snow between rock and the shrinking glacier remnant — usually the crux; carry an ice axe, and it can be bypassed 100-200 ft lower via a rock finger if snow is firm.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path up the broadening ridge, and where the crest narrows above roughly 6,800 ft drop onto the broad benches on the north side rather than staying on top. The path fades into scree and talus as you near the toe of the glacier remnant; traverse along its upper edge to get past several rock pinnacles, assessing the ice before committing to it. Cross the moat between rock and ice — it is hard snow more often than not, which is why an axe belongs on this route, and if it is too firm it can be turned a hundred feet or two lower on a finger of rock.

waypoints.name: Notch below the false summit
waypoints.note: Gain this notch via a V-shaped Class 3.5 slot (some parties belay it), then traverse a ledge west to a wide corner leading up to the false summit.
waypoints.directions: Above the moat, gain the notch through a V-shaped slot of about Class 3.5. It is short but steep and exposed enough that parties often put a rope on it, and it is distinctly harder to reverse than to climb. From the notch, traverse a ledge west to the wide corner that leads up to the false summit.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Peak
waypoints.note: Class 3 scramble on solid rock from the false summit to the true summit block; sweeping views of Mt. Baker, Mt. Shuksan, and north into Canada.
waypoints.directions: From the false summit the true summit looks worse than it is. Downclimb loose ledges to the col between the two, then scramble the summit block on solid, glacier-polished rock — Class 3, with a short gabled section of ridge where the exposure is real on both sides. This is out-and-back ground, so everything climbed here has to be reversed on tired legs.
